@@84898185 <p> The CEO of German utility giant E.ON has called on the German government to intervene to keep down the costs of renewable electricity and " fast-track " the energy transition . <p> Johannes Teyssen said the government needs to cap the tariff added to customer bills to pay for the country 's renewable support schemes , known as the " EEG levy . " Any shortfall in that support should be covered by federal funding , including proceeds from the new carbon tax , Teyssen said Tuesday . <p> Reduced demand during the coronavirus lockdown , coupled with ample wind and solar generation , has seen German power prices go negative , even more so than usual . So far in 2020 , there have been 179 hours of negative pricing , compared to 212 hours during the whole of 2019 , according to data from Wood Mackenzie . <h> Ongoing challenges for Germany 's renewables market <p> Negative pricing and a stressed grid are not the only challenges threatening Germany 's renewables market . Onshore wind permitting delays , ambiguity over the cap on distributed solar and the high-profile ( but now resolved ) delay of Tesla 's German Gigafactory have all served to hamper the country 's energy-transition ambitions . <p> Permitting an onshore wind project can take two years . The government announced it would remove a 52-gigawatt cap on the nation 's total solar capacity for projects under 750 kilowatts , but the cap has not been officially removed from legislation and the limit is about to be breached . <p> Meanwhile , a series of disputes held up work at Tesla 's factory in Berlin . Environmentalists were unhappy with the impact on a local forest , but construction is now set to begin . <p> " Germany needs to fast-track a climate-friendly investment offensive , " E.ON 's Teyssen said in a statement Tuesday , before going on to compare the current situation to Germany 's economic response to the Berlin Wall falling . <p> " After reunification , Germany had this kind of courage , unfortunately only for a short time . Now , after the enormous damage caused by the pandemic and in view of the even greater potential damage that could be caused by unchecked climate change , Germany needs even more courage to make lasting reforms , " he said . <p> " No grid modernization or climate project should be allowed to languish in a consents process for longer than three years . This is an area where Germany can learn from the corona crisis : Digitalize consultation processes and use online technology to speed up administrative processes , " Teyssen said . <p> E.ON is now focused on providing energy services . Adding value through e-mobility and other emerging offerings will be key to its future . But utilities around Europe are struggling with tight margins and the need the invest in the energy transition . <h> Changes need to protect customers from bill hikes <p> Teyssen said action is needed to deliver on a previous promise from Berlin to cut the EEG levy to 5 euro cents per kilowatt-hour ahead of the new carbon tax being put in place . When combined with falling wholesale prices for fossil fuels , current market dynamics could see the green levy rise to 8 euro cents per kilowatt-hour in order to balance the books . This would hit consumers hard , E.ON warned . <p> " The measures we propose would offer economic relief to companies and the public nationwide , " Teyssen said . " They would also provide substantial impetus to speed up electrification , particularly in the transport and heating sectors . We all hope that the economy recovers rapidly . This , along with the revenue from the carbon tax that Germany has decided to institute , can gradually provide the funding for our proposals . " <p> The new German carbon tax will cover the heating and transport sectors not already participating in the EU-wide Emissions Trading Scheme . Rather than requiring end users to take part , the responsibility falls on those putting the fuels into the supply chain . German power providers LEAG and RWE are also among two of the largest coal producers . <h> Financials not impacted by COVID-19 -- yet <p> E.ON saw only a modest impact to its Q1 results from the coronavirus pandemic , with only the final few weeks of March overlapping with lockdowns in the company 's key markets . Its forecast results for 2020 remain in place , but the company warned that could still change . <p> Q1 was also the first full quarter since E.ON 's merger with Innogy . As a result , sales across the entire group nearly doubled from ? 9.1 billion ( $9.9 billion ) in Q1 2019 to ? 17.7 billion . <p> E.ON is adding another ? 500 million to its investments in e-mobility and digitalization. 
@@31835888 <p> The delayed third round of EU-UK trade negotiations has just started this week , taking place virtually due to the ongoing pandemic . Since March , there has been no tangible progress on crucial issues , fisheries included . The UK insists on a separate free trade agreement , while the EU chief negotiator , Michel Barnier , stressed that the EU would not agree to any economic agreement that does not include balanced , sustainable and long-term fisheries . Only one month remains before a potential high-level decision on the continuation ( or not ) of the talks in June . <p> Fisheries , a relatively small sector , is very prominent because it was made totemic by Brexiteers for " taking back control " and defending " British " fish from the nets of EU fishers . However , fish know no borders and their freedom of movement can not be curtailed . EU and UK fisheries are interdependent ; Europeans seek access to British fishing grounds , while British fishers need European markets to export their seafood . Furthermore , UK small-scale fishers want equity at home , a more fair and sustainable national quota allocation ( always entirely within the UK 's competence , the EU has no power here ) , and not the current concentration of fishing rights in the hands of domestic " Codfather " clans . <p> The clock is ticking . The EU and the UK should reach a deal on fisheries by 1 July if they are to live up to the " best endeavours " they wrote into the Political Declaration in October 2019 . Prime minister Boris Johnson also self-imposed a tight timeline and no prolongation of the transition period , gambling with the possibility of a no-deal scenario on 31 December 2020 with its full economic consequences . <p> The deadlock is most concerning for the fishers on both sides of the Channel , for they will suffer direct consequences of a no-deal , and fish populations are increasingly at risk of an overfishing race to the bottom . Oceana urges both parties to prioritize science-based management , by legally committing to maximum sustainable yield as the limit for exploitation . <p> Facing a dramatically short time window and working to the rhythm marked by Coronavirus , the EU and the UK must choose which approach they will take to the negotiation game : cooperation or defection . <p> Agnes Lisik <p> Oceana <p> The EU and the UK can still turn this particular winter of our discontent into a glorious summer , as Richard III would say . Facing a dramatically short time window and working to the rhythm marked by Coronavirus , the EU and the UK must choose which approach they will take to the negotiation game : cooperation or defection . <p> The prisoner 's dilemma is the best-known game example explaining rational - yet possibly uncooperative and selfish - choices . Let 's conduct a thought experiment where the EU and the UK are the " prisoners , " overfishing is the " crime " and these partners must negotiate with a prosecutor . Each prisoner can either blame the other or tacitly cooperate with the other inmate . There are four possible outcomes : <p> If the EU and the UK each blame the other , both lose and there is no deal ( lose-lose ) . <p> If the EU blames the UK but the UK cooperates , the EU will get the best deal possible and the UK will lose ( win-lose ) . <p> If the EU cooperates but the UK blames the EU , the EU will lose and the UK will get the best deal possible ( lose-win ) . <p> If the EU and the UK both cooperate , both will get a deal , although below their initial expectations ( win-win ) . <p> If we apply this type of game to the EU-UK talks , from the environmental but also the socio-economic point of view , the non-cooperative no-deal scenario is the most destructive one . It inevitably results in uncertainty and competition for shrinking natural resources , leading to deregulation , a return to overfishing and a collapse of fish stocks as a consequence . <p> Scenarios two and three - although possibly a boost to certain political egos and pandering to a domestic audience and rewarding national pride - still do not provide enough cooperation , balance and decision ownership to manage shared fish populations sustainably and successfully in the long-term . It is obvious that the win-win outcome is optimal and should be the joint goal of the negotiators . Science-guided collaboration can bring order and stability , and gains from cooperation will always outweigh payoffs from rivalry . <p> Meanwhile , the long-term emergency that has not vanished is the combination of climate change and biodiversity loss which can result in the real endgame for humanity . <p> Agnes Lisik <p> Oceana <p> Of course , this is an oversimplified model for brevity 's sake . There are two great game-changers disrupting these strategies and they drastically differ in their time horizon . The short to mid-term crisis - which might look more urgent - is the coronavirus pandemic . It dramatically adds the ethical trolley problem to the prisoner 's dilemma , whereby governments must make decisions between their citizens ' lives and the economy . <p> Meanwhile , the long-term emergency that has not vanished is the combination of climate change and biodiversity loss which can result in the real endgame for humanity . Only through transparent international cooperation with ambitious , sustainable and science-based objectives can fisheries and other transboundary issues be addressed . I sincerely hope that " common sense , " that famous British virtue , will eventually triumph and overcome a zero-sum game .

@@31837390 <h> Lakes triple amount of carbon they bury in response to human disruption of global nutrient cycles <p> A new study led by Loughborough University has revealed that lake burial of organic carbon has increased three-fold over the last 100 years in response to human disruption of global nutrient cycles . <p> Professor John Anderson , of the Geography and Environment department in the School of Social Sciences and Humanities , hopes the findings will expand our understanding of global carbon storage and the role lakes play in this , as the burial process was previously considered not important . <p> The research , published in Science Advances , was undertaken in an attempt to account for some of the gaps in the global carbon budget . <p> The global carbon budget looks at the amount of carbon produced on a global scale and where it ends up . <p> In theory , the amount of carbon released by human activities -- such as burning fossil fuels and chopping down trees -- and the amount of carbon taken up by oceans , soils and the atmosphere , should balance . <p> However , the numbers do not quite add up and part of the budget is considering ' missing ' as we are unable to account for where some of the carbon has gone . <p> This is an issue as balancing the budget is an important part of understanding the contemporary carbon cycle , which scientists analyze to predict future levels of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere and its greenhouse effect . <p> Though it is known that all lakes bury carbon , little attention has been paid to this fact and previous lake studies have only considered how carbon is transferred from land to the water . <p> Professor Anderson 's research , which is in collaboration with Dr. Adam Heathcote and Dr. Daniel Engstrom , of the Science Museum of Minnesota ( SMM ) , and the Globocarb consortium ( a team of 20 academics from institutions around the world ) , is the first study to explore whether lake carbon burial rates have increased over the last 100 years across the globe . <p> Lakes bury carbon as organic matter -- matter that has come from a recently living organisms ( for example , decomposing aquatic vegetation ) , which is roughly 50 percent organic carbon . <p> The matter sinks to the bottom of lakes and remains there as a brown-looking sludge . Oceans and estuaries also bury carbon -- but not as much as lakes in relative terms . <p> To assess how burial rates have changed over time , Professor Anderson and the research team looked at sediment cores taken from 516 natural lakes across the globe . <p> As well as looking at data and samples from different countries and continents -- including the UK , South America , Sweden , Denmark and Canada -- they also looked at lakes in Earth 's different vegetation zones -- known as ' biomes ' -- such as the rainforest , savannah and tundra . <p> Professor Anderson and the team calculated the age of the sediment cores using radiometric dating ( 210Pb ) -- a technique used to date materials based on the known decay rate of the radioactive elements they contain -- and they also calculated the organic content of the sediment . <p> Their approach was particularly novel as they used an enhancement of the 210Pb dating method that acts as a focusing correction . <p> This method allowed them to standardize the burial rate across all lakes -- which is important as lakes vary in size and sediment is not distributed uniformly -- and then calculate how much organic carbon is buried by all lakes in one geographic area . <p> From their analysis , the team found : <p> The total global carbon burial rate by lakes has increased from 0.05 PgC yr-1 to 0.12 PgC yr-1 ( where 1 petagram ( Pg ) of carbon ( C ) is equivalent to 1 billion metric tons of carbon , or 3.67 billion metric tons of CO2 ) over the last 100 years <p> Across all biomes , burial rates have tripled , including four-fold increases in lakes in tropical grasslands and forests -- which reflects the high level of human disturbance in the tropics during the 20thcentury <p> Lakes in the boreal biomes ( forest areas of northern Eurasia and northern North America ) contribute to the largest proportion of global carbon burial rate due to their large coverage , but they are closely followed by lakes in tropical forests and then lakes located in grasslands and the savannah . <p> The team also found that the increase in burial rates is largely in response to the major physical transformation of the Earth 's surface over the last 100-200 years . <p> Forests play a huge role in the carbon cycle and when they are cut down , not only does carbon absorption cease , but the carbon stored in the trees is released into the atmosphere through burning or decomposition . <p> Human activity in the 1950s resulted in rapid land-cover changes and the removal of forests , massively impacting the carbon cycle . <p> The researchers found most biomes increased lake carbon burial from the late 19th century onwards , meaning lakes were responding to these major changes in the earth 's biogeochemistry . <p> As well increasing burial rates to offset land-based carbon emissions , the researchers also found that human disruption to the nitrogen cycle and other nutrient cycles impacted burial rates . <p> Fertilizers and nutrient additives are used in farming to help crops grow and they often enter lakes and streams through runoff and soil erosion . <p> The same nutrients that help crops grow also increases the growth of aquatic plants , which in turn increases the amount of decaying plant matter in lakes and therefore the amount of buried carbon . <p> The team found in areas with intensive agricultural and substantial nutrient subsides through fertilizer use -- such as areas that were mixed forests and grasslands in Europe and North America prior to land use changes -- lake burial rates have increased three-fold since the start of the 20th century . <p> Of the research , which is shared in a paper titled " Anthropogenic alteration of nutrient supply increases the global freshwater carbon sink , " Professor Anderson said : " Carbon burial in lakes is a sink in the context of the modern carbon cycle , it can be thought as offsetting the effects of anthropogenic CO2 release . <p> " I hope this research makes people aware that burial rates are an important part of the linked terrestrial-aquatic carbon cycle and that rates have increased . <p> " It also highlights that climate change is not a significant component of this increased burial rate , it is mainly land-use and associated changes in nutrient use that are the main drivers . " <p> Professor Anderson hopes to build on this research by better constraining the burial rates in the Arctic -- an area with many lakes but which is relatively understudied . <p> This study found carbon burial rates to be low in Artic lakes , but the rates may increase rapidly in the future as a result of melting permafrost ( ground that remains permanently frozen ) and this is important given the Arctic is where much of the earth 's organic carbon is stored . <p> Citation : Lakes triple amount of carbon they bury in response to human disruption of global nutrient cycles ( 2020 , April 28 ) retrieved 15 May 2020 from https : **39;1367;TOOLONG ... @@84913588 <h> Posted ! <h> Join the Conversation <h> Comments <p> Welcome to our new and improved comments , which are for subscribers only . This is a test to see whether we can improve the experience for you . You do not need a Facebook profile to participate . <p> You will need to register before adding a comment . Typed comments will be lost if you are not logged in . <p> Please be polite . It 's OK to disagree with someone 's ideas , but personal attacks , insults , threats , hate speech , advocating violence and other violations can result in a ban . If you see comments in violation of our community guidelines , please report them . <h> Orchid mystique : Tallahassee Orchid Society grows a legacy <p> If you are an orchid lover and have questions on how to grow or procure healthy orchid plants , come to the Orchid Club meeting in Tallahassee and explore the world of orchids . <p> The Tallahassee Orchid Society was established by a group of orchid lovers in 1965 with an intention of protecting these vanishing species . The society has been educating people and promoting orchid cultivation ever since . They are also determined to continue the legacy of maintaining orchid species passed on to them by fellow orchid growers who are no longer with us or hybrids developed several decades ago . <p> Several members in the club still own the plants once grown by founding members . You can also be a part of this orchid legacy by joining the Tallahassee Orchid Society . <p> Orchids are an enchanting flowering plants but growing orchids can present a challenge to even the greenest thumbs . <p> You must be patient and learn a few tips to grow them successfully . Online is one source but , for regular growing guidance your local club or local nurseries will know what works best in this area . <p> Paphiopedilum growing in the living room ( Photo : Hemanth V. Setty ) <p> Orchids can be successfully grown in the greenhouse . Most of the professional growers or hobbyists own a greenhouse where one can maintain a controlled environment . Not everyone can afford a greenhouse and the majority of the orchid enthusiasts either grow orchids inside their house or on a patio . <p> I have been successfully growing cattleyas , dendrobiums , vandas , bulbophyllums , phalaenopsis , encyclias , epidendrums and vanilla orchids inside my house and on the patio . There are few important tips that you must know before starting your hobby . <p> Most of the orchids are epiphytes and have aerial roots that cling tightly to the host plant in nature . They prefer to live on the shaded , west side of the tree , where it takes advantages of the greatest amount of humidity . Like most of the plants , orchids depend on their environment which influences their developmental process . External circumstances such as light , temperature , air and soil/medium and nutrition must be favorable for effectively growing and blooming of orchids . <p> Happy growing Vanda on the patio . ( Photo : Hemanth V. Setty ) <p> Light is one of the important factors which delivers the energy necessary for plant development . When growing inside the house one should consider the light intensity during temperate spring and in summer months . During summer months when the intensity is too strong , a southern/western expose is only good when the orchid plant can be provided with enough shade , such as from blinds , shades or curtains . It is not too difficult to gauge light requirements for every orchid . <p> Leaf color is good indicator , if it is dark green it means that plant is not receiving adequate light . If a plant is receiving sufficient light than the leaf will be light green in color . Too little light causes weak growth , and often is the reason it is not blooming when it should . <p> Temperature is another important factor . For most orchids , temperature between 60 - 82 F is ideal . If you are comfortable , your plants will also be comfortable . <p> Temperature around orchid plants depends on air movement and the place where your plants are either on windowsill or kitchen counter , bathroom , living room or patio . In most cases , day temperature of 75-90 F and 59-65 F night temperatures are ideal but many orchids can go much warmer , and do fine outside . Bring your plants indoors from the patio if the temperature drops below 55 F. <p> Phalaenopsis on the kitchen countertop . ( Photo : Hemanth V. Setty ) <p> Like light and temperature , humidity of air and soil plays an important part in successful orchid cultivation . You can use a hygrometer to measure the humidity . Most of the time the room or house humidity will be around 35% . If a windowsill is used provide additional humidity , especially during winter months . <p> You can either use a humidifier or a large bowl filled with water to increase humidity . But do not place the pot in the container with water , as it will drown the plant . You can likewise mist the plant with water to increase humidity . In summer months , provide additional air circulation by using either table or ceiling fans . Stagnant , heavy air is detrimental to orchids . <p> Like surrounding air humidity , moisture in the medium is also important . Too much water is harmful . Overwatering is the quickest way to kill an orchid . <p> A good rule of thumb is -- as little as possible , but as much as necessary . The best indicator is again the leaf . Yellowing of the leaves means too much water or roots rotting . It also correlates if air humidity is too high . Orchids do not want watering every day . Allowing for a short period of drying out is better than drowning them . Water once a week to 10 days in winter and once or twice a week in summer is ideal . <p> Phalaenopsis orchids must have only the roots watered , as water left in the center of leaves can cause crown rot and kill the plant . Pots can dry out at different rates , especially if different sizes or in different mixes or pot material . <p> Water quality also plays an important role in successful orchid cultivation . I use tap water for my orchids but , well water is also fine . Water thoroughly and allow to drain well . Do not use softened water , as the salt is toxic to the plants . Also , it should be at about room temperature . Tap water can be very cold in winter , and phalaenopsis can be damaged if too cold . Also , never use ice cubes . I have never seen them in the jungle . Save them for your lemonade . <p> Potting material and repotting are also a vital factor . The potting mixture used should allow air/water to move through it . At the same time , it should retain sufficient moisture and nutrients . I use a commercial orchid mixture which contains bark/charcoal/perlite , available locally . To that I add a little extra sphagnum moss to retain moisture . <p> I usually repot when I see plants pot-bound or decline in health . I do not have the issue of diseases and pests . I always quarantine new plants and wipe leaves once a month either with soap or 70% alcohol to remove any debris or bugs . Scale and mealy bugs are the most common pests and can be controlled this way . It is important to regularly inspect your plants for any issues . <p> By growing orchids , you are indirectly helping in their conservation . <p> Many orchid species in the wild all over the world are on the verge of extinction due to overcollecting , habitat loss and climate change . Your garden could become a survival place for orchids.There are several native orchids that grow in the panhandle of Florida , mostly on the ground , and not in trees . <p> Tallahassee Orchid Society members at their 50th Annual Orchid Show in 2016 , what an achievement . ( Photo : Tallahassee Orchid Society ) <p> You can become part of this orchid legacy by joining the club . Regular club activities involve invited guest speakers , member presentations , show-and-tell with member 's plants . The best part is interaction with fellow growers . <p> The club hosts an annual orchid show every year in April . Reputable Florida orchid and supply vendors participate in the show and bring ones that are great to grow . This year the 54th Annual Orchid Show was canceled due to the coronavirus pandemic . <p> The Tallahassee Orchid Society meet monthly on the second Thursday at 7 p.m. in the Jubilee Cottage at Goodwood Museum and Gardens ( www.goodwoodmuseum.org/ ) . Our website is www.tallyorchid.org/ . Please like us on Facebook **42;459;TOOLONG . **99;503; Dr. Hemanth Setty is a long-time gardener , numismatist , philatelist and member of the Tallahassee Orchid Society.Contact him at **29;605;TOOLONG 
@@84917699 <h> Posted ! <h> Join the Conversation <h> Comments <p> Welcome to our new and improved comments , which are for subscribers only . This is a test to see whether we can improve the experience for you . You do not need a Facebook profile to participate . <p> You will need to register before adding a comment . Typed comments will be lost if you are not logged in . <p> Please be polite . It 's OK to disagree with someone 's ideas , but personal attacks , insults , threats , hate speech , advocating violence and other violations can result in a ban . If you see comments in violation of our community guidelines , please report them . <p> One of the Roosevelt Irrigation District 's wells ( bottom center ) sits next to an auto shop at Van Buren Street and 28th Drive in Phoenix . ( Photo : Michael Chow and Thomas Hawthorne/The Republic ) <p> A long-delayed cleanup of toxic chemicals in the groundwater beneath Phoenix could get a boost if the federal Environmental Protection Agency agrees to Arizona 's request to take over the work . <p> The EPA is considering a request to add the area , called the West Van Buren site , to its national priorities list by making it part of an adjacent federal Superfund site or by establishing a new Superfund site . It 's unclear how long the EPA might take to decide whether it will oversee the cleanup of contaminated groundwater . <p> While Arizona awaits an answer , some environmental advocates have called for the state to pay for treating the water to remove hazardous chemicals , arguing officials have an obligation to address the problem now . <p> The West Van Buren site is part of a larger polluted section of Phoenix that stretches across 15 miles of the city , making the area one of the biggest zones of contaminated groundwater in the country . <p> The West Van Buren site borders the federal Superfund site around the Motorola 52nd Street Plant , where cleanup efforts have been underway for three decades . <p> Industrial chemicals soaked into the ground in central Phoenix during the 1950s , ' 60s and ' 70s.For years , industries from factories to dry cleaners dumped solvents around their plantsand left the groundwater polluted with harmful chemicals including trichloroethylene ( TCE ) and tetrachloroethylene ( PCE ) . <p> A water treatment system for removing toxic chemicals stands beside a drilling rig and a well at the I-17 frontage road and Van Buren Street in Phoenix . Consultants for Roosevelt Irrigation District have operated treatment systems on four wells . One of the wells has been undergoing maintenance . ( Photo : Michael Chow and Thomas Hawthorne/The Republic ) <p> For years , the toxic plume has been gradually moving through the aquifer beneath the city . <p> But the polluted water is n't flowing to households . Instead , it 's pumped from wells into canals that carry it to fields of alfalfa and cotton in the West Valley . <p> Tests have shown that , as the water gushes into canals , it releases measurable amounts of TCE and PCE into the air . <p> There is debate about whether these chemicals are becoming airborne at levels that could pose health risks in the surrounding community . State environmental regulators have said the chemicals are entering the air in such small amounts that there is no risk to public health . Some critics have questioned that conclusion . <p> There has also been disagreement about how environmental agencies should handle the cleanup , and about whether Arizona should be prioritizing more funding for the site . <p> Until last year , environmental consultants working for Roosevelt Irrigation District , or RID , had been operating small water treatment plants at three wells , removing the chemicals from some of the most contaminated water . <p> This treatment system , on a well at 35th Avenue and Sherman Street in Phoenix , was was recently shut down due to lack of funds . ( Photo : Mark Henle/The Republic ) <p> The funding that had been available to operate the systems ran out last year . Since the end of last summer , the treatment plants have been shut down . <p> The environmental consultants , with the firm Synergy Environmental , say it 's crucial to treat the water from these wells to keep the toxins out of the air . <p> " It 's unbelievable to us that the state wo n't address a site so obviously in need of remediation , " said Dennis Shirley , one of the consultants with Synergy Environmental . Without funding for treatment , he said , more chemicals will be released into the air as water is pumped from the wells . <p> Officials at the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality strongly disagreed . <p> " For the groundwater 's current use -- irrigation -- there is no significant risk to public health , " said Caroline Oppleman , ADEQ 's communications administrator . She said that includes no significant health risk from vapor inhalation . <p> Oppleman cited data gathered by ADEQ and by Synergy Environmental . She also cited a 2015 report by the Arizona Department of Health Services , which analyzed exposure scenarios including inhalation and concluded the water in the area " is not expected to harm people 's health . " <p> In an emailed response to questions from The Arizona Republic , Oppleman said ADEQ and " responsible parties " have already conducted significant cleanup work . Those efforts have involved removing 13,000 pounds of volatile organic compounds , or VOCs , and 3,100 tons of soil , as well as treating about 118 million gallons of groundwater . <p> Records released by ADEQ show the state has received about $4.9 million from eight companies in settlements related to the West Van Buren site . Since 1999 , records show the state has spent about $7.3 million on cleanup efforts at the site , though spending has dwindled during the past several years . <p> Shirley has argued ADEQ should have prioritized more funding for the site and pursued polluters to get them to pay for the cleanup . He said the agency 's inaction represents an environmental injustice for the area 's largely Hispanic community . <p> Shirley has repeatedly written to ADEQ to request funding to keep the treatment plants operating . In a February letter to Laura Malone , director of the agency 's waste programs division , Shirley said that since 2012 , the treatment plants at four wells have treated more than 9 billion gallons of contaminated groundwater and removed an estimated 3,700 pounds of VOCs . <p> " RID has exhausted all funds available to continue treatment at these wells , " Shirley said in the letter . <p> Noting that the state 's program is now fully funded , he requested $1.2 million to keep the treatment systems running this year . <p> Joel Peterson of the firm Synergy Environmental works at the treatment system at one of the Roosevelt Irrigation District 's wells , at 35th Avenue and Sherman Street in Phoenix . ( Photo : Mark Henle/The Republic ) <p> If the water is n't treated , Shirley wrote , it creates a " direct pathway of public exposure . " <p> ADEQ officials disagreed , saying data collected for a 2011 report show the amount of chemicals released is minuscule . For comparison , they cited an estimate that cars in the Phoenix area release approximately 100,000 pounds of VOCs into the air per day . <p> As for Shirley 's funding request , Oppleman said , since the EPA has n't yet responded to Arizona 's proposal to expand the Superfund site , " it would be premature to make large expenditures of State dollars , especially now , when we fully believe it is a federal responsibility . " <p> Officials with the EPA have said they are n't aware of any data that indicates people are being exposed to unsafe levels of contamination . <p> But the environmental consultants , as well as some environmental activists , have continued to question what they say are the potential long-term health risks of airborne TCE , and the lack of funding for cleanup work . <p> " It certainly makes one wonder why ADEQ has funded so many smaller groundwater cleanup actions , at lower-priority sites where there is no public exposure , and yet fails to provide funding to the largest groundwater contamination site in the state , " said Joel Peterson , an engineer and Shirley 's partner at Synergy Environmental . <p> Joel Peterson of the firm Synergy Environmental bleeds air from the treatment system on a well at 35th Avenue and Sherman Street in Phoenix . ( Photo : Mark Henle/The Republic ) <p> The environmental nonprofit Do n't Waste Arizona has also voiced concerns . Scott Meyer , the group 's president , wrote to ADEQ officials last month , urging the agency to use available funds to continue treating the water and removing TCE . <p> " This site is the ONLY site in Arizona where contaminants will be dumped directly into the community 's ambient air , " Meyer wrote . He said releasing carcinogens into the air brings added risk for people in the community . <p> TCE has been linked to kidney cancer , liver cancer and lymphoma , and studies have found harmful effects on the immune system and the nervous system , and risks of heart defects in developing fetuses . The federal government classifies PCE as a likely carcinogen . <p> " There is no coincidence that this site is home to an ethnic minority population , " Meyer said . He said failing to protect the community constitutes " environmental racism " and a " blatant civil rights violation . " <p> Oppleman said those accusations are unfounded . <p> " No data support a claim that ambient air is affected significantly by vapors from RID groundwater pumping , " she said in her email . Cleanup activities are prioritized , Oppleman said , " to protect public health and the environment and are based on mitigating exposure risks . " <p> The groundwater is n't being used as a source of drinking water , Oppleman said , and people in the area are being supplied clean , safe water . <h> Arizona 's request to the EPA <p> Two years ago , in April 2018 , Arizona officials wrote to the EPA asking the agency to consider expanding the western boundary of the Motorola Superfund site to include parts of the West Van Buren site . <p> Misael Cabrera , the director of ADEQ , said in the letter that his request was based on data showing the plume of chemicals had migrated from the Motorola site into the state 's site . <p> Cabrera asked the EPA to take over only parts of the West Van Buren site where evidence points to contamination connected to the Motorola site . He said if the EPA decides not to extend the site 's boundary , Arizona would ask the agency to consider listing the West Van Buren area as its own Superfund site . <p> To support its request , ADEQ submitted a memo in December detailing an analysis that showed TCE contamination originating from the Motorola site has " migrated a significant distance " into the West Van Buren site , well beyond the Seventh Avenue boundary and at least to 56th Avenue . <p> " This represents over 5 miles of plume migration , " ADEQ 's Malone wrote in a letter summarizing the analysis . <p> Malone told Enrique Manzanilla , director of the EPA 's regional Superfund division , that ADEQ " is confident in its position " and has provided adequate documentation to expand the Motorola Superfund site . <p> Contamination from the Motorola site is " the last remaining major contributor " to the West Van Buren site , Oppleman said . Because the groundwater is connected , she said , ADEQ environmental engineers and scientists " believe a combined solution may be more cost effective than separate solutions " and could also streamline the cleanup . <p> The EPA is completing a preliminary assessment to determine whether the West Van Buren site may qualify to be added to the national Superfund list , either as a new site or as part of the Motorola site , said Denise Adamic , a press officer in the EPA 's regional office in San Francisco . She said the review involves gathering information to evaluate " whether the site poses a threat to human health and the environment . " <p> To conclude the review , Adamic said , the EPA must finish evaluating more than 30 years of data , including " whether that data indicates that the original release from the former Motorola 52nd Street plant reached , and is responsible for , the groundwater contamination . " <p> She said the EPA does n't have an estimate of how long the review will take . <h> ' They 've got to be treating this stuff ' <p> The groundwater in this part of Phoenix flows gradually westward . The contaminated water moves underground beneath mobile home parks , supermarkets , schools and auto shops along West Van Buren Street . <p> Orlando Ruelas lives in the area and works as an environmental services specialist , regularly replacing carbon filter media in water treatment systems . He has done this work at various plants across the Phoenix area , including the ones that Synergy Environmental recently shut down . <p> Ruelas said he hopes to see the authorities move forward with the cleanup . Two of his kids go to school next to a well where the water flows untreated into a canal . He said he 's concerned about the potential health risks . <p> " That 's one of the reasons I 'm trying to work as hard as I can to move out of this place , " Ruelas said . " I 've seen the test results . I mean , they 've got to be treating this stuff . " <p> Ruelas often works at contaminated sites in the Scottsdale and Goodyear areas , where he said the problems are being addressed . <p> " Why can we not do it right here in central Phoenix ? " Ruelas said . " Why are they not taking care of this site ? " <p> If it were added to the national list , the West Van Buren site would join nine other Superfund sites in Arizona . Those include the Apache Powder Co. in St. David , the Iron King Mine and Humboldt Smelter facilities in Yavapai County , the Indian Bend Wash area in Scottsdale , and the closed Williams Air Force Base near Chandler , among others . <p> For years , disagreements over cleanup approaches and legal fights over costs have swirled around the West Van Buren site . The disputes have included accusations by Phoenix water officials and others that RID and its allies were attempting a " water grab , " planning to take the water once it was cleaned up and sell it to cities in the West Valley . <p> Alongside these disputes , Roosevelt Irrigation District was until recently in a court case with Salt River Project over its ability to pump groundwater in the coming years . <p> The water rights dispute has been resolved under a contract extension that will allow RID to continue using its wells to deliver water for agricultural irrigation , said Scott Harelson , an SRP spokesperson . <p> The agreement will allow RID to keep supplying water to farms " on a declining basis over time , " Harelson said , until the area of irrigated farmland -- now about 24,000 acres -- decreases to 2,000 acres as fields are replaced with suburban growth . <p> The resolution of this dispute will allow SRP and Phoenix to continue working with other agencies " to finalize and fund a regional groundwater remedy , " Harelson said . <p> The long-running disputes have also included disagreements over cleanup approaches between companies blamed for the contamination and other parties . Oppleman said these disagreements may mean the " joint and several " liability approach of the federal Superfund program will be faster . <p> Under the federal Superfund law , any single " potentially responsible party " can be held liable for an entire cleanup . Under Arizona 's " proportionate liability " approach , in contrast , each party is liable for paying cleanup costs forits share of the contamination . <p> Some of the companies and agencies that have been identified as " potentially responsible parties " belong to an association called the West Van Buren Working Group . In 2014 , lawyers for the group asked ADEQ to investigate about 3,800 other potentially responsible parties in the area . <p> They included more than 1,000 auto repair shops , as well as hundreds of metalworking and metal-plating businesses , dry cleaners , electronics manufacturers , chemical facilities and other businesses . <p> ADEQ has said this request to investigate 3,800 potential contributors could significantly slow down the process . <h> Cleanup would yield drinking water <p> In the long term , cleaning up the groundwater could help provide an additional water source for Phoenix and other cities in the Valley . <p> Phoenix now depends mostly on water from the Colorado River , the Salt River and the Verde River . In a typical year , water pumped from wells makes up only about 2% of the city 's supply . But city officials have said groundwater will be a key piece of the city 's future water supplies as climate change takes a growing toll on sources of surface water . <p> In the past , Phoenix water officials have had to shut down wells in some areas when contamination was detected . According to a 2011 water plan , the city shut down six wells with high levels of TCE after officials began testing for the chemical in the 1980s . In all , the document said , Phoenix shut down more than 60 wells between 1981 and 2000 due to elevated levels of various substances . <p> Other contaminants that taint groundwater in parts of the city include heavy metals , pesticides , and nitrates that leached into aquifers years ago from fertilizers on farmlands . Bringing these contaminated wells back online to supply drinking water would require investments in treatment systems . <p> One of the Roosevelt Irrigation District 's wells stands next to homes near 32nd Ave . and Van Buren Street in Phoenix . ( Photo : Mark Henle/The Republic ) <p> Tests have shown the groundwater in the West Van Buren area contains chemicals at levels exceeding safe drinking water standards . <p> The latest groundwater monitoring report , published in February , said consultants sampled 84 wells for chemicals and found 22 wells had levels of toxins exceeding standards -- either TCE , PCE , 1,1-dichloroethene , or a combination of these chemicals . <p> State legislators have backed ADEQ 's request to the EPA , saying expanding the Superfund site to include portions of the West Van Buren site would make for a " speedier and more efficient " cleanup . <p> The EPA has provided funds to combat other environmental problems in the Phoenix area . This month , the agency announced $1.4 million in federal grants to clean up contaminated lands , among them polluted sites along the Salt River . <p> Shirley , of Synergy Environmental , has asked federal officials to get involved . <p> " We urge immediate EPA action , or some form of collaboration with ADEQ , to provide continued funding " to run the water treatment systems , Shirley wrote in a February letter . <p> Do n't Waste Arizona has also urged the EPA to step in . <p> In a letter last year , Meyer said the site " has been shamefully neglected over the last 30 years " due to delays in determining the responsible parties and their liabilities . <p> Meyer said the federal Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry should conduct a risk assessment for TCE in the air . <p> In addition to releases from wells , TCE vapors can sometimes emerge from contaminated soil and pollute the air inside homes and buildings . <p> In the West Van Buren area , ADEQ officials have said the water table is relatively deep , from 94 feet to 144 feet underground . Oppleman said the agency 's modeling " shows very low , if any , risk " of vapors tainting indoor air . <p> Meyer pointed to studies of " vapor intrusion " from the Motorola 52nd Street Superfund site , saying " TCE is coming up through the ground " and contributing to toxic air . <p> Activists with Do n't Waste Arizona have been commenting on the Motorola site cleanup since their group was incorporated in 1992 . Meyer said officials have never explained why Seventh Avenue became an arbitrary dividing line splitting the federal site and the state-administered site . <p> Meyer said he wants the federal government to take over so the cleanup actually happens . The way things stand now , he said , if it 's left to the state , he fears a cleanup will never occur . <p> Environmental coverage on azcentral.com and in The Arizona Republic is supported by a grant from the Nina Mason Pulliam Charitable Trust . @@31839580 <h> California 's budget cuts threaten environmental spending <p> The Rundown : Top headlines today : May 14 , 2020Stay up to date on the developing stories making headlines.The Associated Press <p> SACRAMENTO , Calif. -- California Gov . Gavin Newsom 's proposed budget cuts include canceling billions of dollars in climate change spending , a blow to environmental advocates who look to the state as a stopgap for the Trump administration 's weakening of federal protections . <p> In January , Newsom proposed a $12 billion " climate budget " that , over the next five years , would offer incentives for companies to convert to electric vehicles , give low-interest loans to businesses to clean up their practices and spend billions on projects preparing for floods , droughts and wildfires . <p> But Thursday , Newsom proposed eliminating most of the foundation for those programs to balance a budget that will have an estimated $54.3 billion deficit . The economic downturn has been brought by a statewide stay-at-home order to limit the spread of the coronavirus . The order has closed most businesses for two months , putting more than 4.5 million people out of work and sending state tax collections plummeting . <p> The proposed cuts come as the state is battling the Trump administration over water quality and auto emissions , among other environmental issues . <p> " At a time when the Trump administration is mounting an unprecedented assault on environmental and public health protection , it 's absolutely devastating and horrifying , " said Kassie Siegel , director of the Climate Law Institute at the Center for Biological Diversity . <p> The Newsom administration says the cuts represent " unprecedented times " that have forced the state to " make sacrifices that we did n't think six months ago we would have to do . " The administration chose to protect programs to clean up the air in disadvantaged communities and to provide safe drinking water . <p> " All the leaders around the world from Germany to Denmark to Japan are all suffering similar economic fates , " said Jared Blumenfeld , secretary of the California Environmental Protection Agency . " What California is doing is prioritizing and making sure , as the governor said , our values come first . " <p> The biggest cut was scrapping a proposal to borrow $4.75 billion to prepare the state for climate-change disasters like sea level rise that threatens the coastal cities and devastating wildfires that have destroyed tens of thousands of buildings and killed more than 100 people . <p> That proposal could be revived in the Legislature , where lawmakers view it as a type of economic stimulus to create jobs during a coronavirus-induced economic downturn . But they would first have to convince Newsom not to veto it over cost concerns . <p> Newsom canceled a $250 million contribution to the " climate catalyst fund , " aimed at jump starting investment in technology to help clean up private sector polluters . <p> But the most ironic impact is on the state 's " cap and trade " program , which requires big businesses to purchase credits that allow them to pollute . Coronavirus-related closures since mid-March have shut down most businesses and kept cars off the road , leading to a dramatic improvement in air quality . But it 's also reduced the demand for credits , meaning the state is likely to make less money when it sells them . <p> That means less money for a host of programs offering incentives for companies to convert their diesel-powered fleets -- one of the largest sources of air pollution -- to electric vehicles . <p> " The good news is emissions are decreasing . However , there is a lot of funding that has occurred in the past that may not occur in the future as a result of that , " Blumenfeld said . <p> The Newsom administration canceled a plan to hire 53 more people to regulate the state 's oil and gas industry . The cut surprised environmental advocates because the new employees would have been paid for not by state income tax collections , but by fees paid from the oil and gas industry itself . <p> " Oil and gas won , " said Kathryn Phillips , director of Sierra Club California . " But people who breathe and live near ports are losing . " <p> State Oil and Gas Supervisor Uduak-Joe Ntuk said the economic downturn and " historically low demand for oil and gas " has impacted operators , " many of whom are facing layoffs and cutbacks . <p> " Requesting additional fees during this crisis would be a difficult challenge , " he said . " We all need to stretch our limited resources , and CalGEM is committed to continuing its critical core enforcement and regulatory work with its current resources . "

@@84948585 <h> What does Tropical Storm Arthur mean for South Jersey , Memorial Day ? <p> For the sixth year in a row , a named tropical system has formed in the Atlantic Hurricane Basin before the official start of the season June 1 . <p> The good news is that South Jersey will receive no direct impact from this . However , in conjunction with a large , upper level low pressure system to our west , minor to moderate coastal flooding , winds , high seas , some rain and beach erosion will begin Monday night , and last into much of the week . <p> For those away from the bays and beaches , expect Monday night through Thursday to bring cool weather , with sun and shower . So , it will be a low impact event for those of you there . <p> To help you prepare for what 's to come , as well as what lies ahead to Memorial Day Weekend , here 's a breakdown of what you need to know . <h> Track of Arthur <p> Tropical Storm Arthur , as of Sunday afternoon , is expected to move northward and either make landfall or pass very close to the Outer Banks during the day Monday . From there , it will make a right turn off the Virginia coast Monday night and slowly head toward Bermuda , where it will be near Thursday . <h> Timing <p> This varies depending on the impacts . However , expect strong onshore winds to develop late Monday . The high surf , seas and coastal flooding may not end until late Thursday . Rain showers from the upper level low mentioned above should not exit until Saturday . <h> Coastal Flooding <p> Be prepared to move your cars and not drive through the flooded water . Spotty minor flood stage will begin with the Tuesday morning high tide . By the Tuesday evening high tide , widespread coastal flooding will be likely . This should be minor , borderline moderate , flood stage . Minor flood stage is the nuisance flooding we see many times a year . Moderate flood stage is when water inundation begins . Roads , more than just the " usual " ones , have water them and some roads can be closed for hours at a time . <p> Any high tide Wednesday or Thursday have the potential for coastal flooding . The exact details will still need to be worked out and there is some hope that the morning high tides just stay outside of flood stage . However , do anticipate more minor to borderline moderate flood stage for now . <h> Everyone in New Jersey can uses this tool to estimate street flooding . <p> Input the tide height above the mean higher high water ( MHHW ) value , using a website like the Stevens ' Institute of Technology , and get an estimate of how much coastal flooding you will see during the high tide . <p> The Surging Seas Risk Finder by ClimateCentral , an independent organization in New Jersey researching and reporting the facts about climate change and its impact on the public , is meant to show the rising waters from climate change . However , it can also be used for specific coastal flooding events . <h> Cape May County residents can use a local flood mapper tool <p> Cape May County has an interactive web tool that allows you to see roughly what flooding will be like , down to street level , in the county . <p> The flood mapper tool allows you to visualize the coastal flooding event by clicking on the region of the county ( North , Central and South ) you are searching for , clicking on the tide height and moving about the map . <p> Current tide heights are listed for Ocean City , Sea Isle City and Cape May . However , to view what the flood will look like for a future flood event , the Mid Atlantic River Forecasting Center will help . Using the MARFC page , click on the tide forecast for Ocean City and/or Cape May . For Sea Isle City , you can extrapolate the flood stage forecast in one of the other two sites for there . <h> Out on the water <p> Fortunately , perhaps , this is all coming before the Memorial Day Weekend and the unofficial beginning on summer . Seas out in the Atlantic Ocean will be between 8 and 14 feet from Monday night , right on through Thursday night . The worst of the seas will come between Tuesday night and Thursday itself . Seas will be 5 to 8 feet Friday , diminishing more into the weekend . On the Delaware Bay , expect 3 to 5 foot waves between Monday night and Thursday . <p> Rough surf will be likely over the next several days as well . Expect minor beach erosion at the coasts as the persistent winds eat away at the shore . <h> Wind <p> Winds will fluctuate between east-northeast and east-southeast Monday and Friday . Wind damage will not be likely . Though what it lacks in intensity will be made up in the persistent duration of the winds . You 'll want to secure lawn chairs or any loose objects . <p> At the shore , sustained winds will be 20 to 30 mph starting Monday night and ending Wednesday night . Gusts up to 40 mph will be likely at times . Usually , 45 mph is when you begin to see power outages and downed tree limbs . <p> On the mainland , expect it to be breezy . Sustained winds will be 15-25 mph , with gusts to 35 mph . For a state used to high wind events by now , this should be a breeze . <h> Rain <p> No flooding rains look likely . A rain shower will be likely at any point between Monday night and Saturday . However , most of this time will be dry . In fact , you 'll even get sunshine at times . <p> The wettest points look to be Monday night , as Arthur makes its closest approach to the area . Even here , only the shore is guaranteed any rain . Tuesday and Wednesday have the best potential of being 100% dry , as high pressure tries to poke in from the north . <p> As the high pressure breaks down , Thursday through Saturday all can see showers . This exact amount will be dependent on the track of the upper level low pressure , as it will finally move through here . However , I do believe not washout will be likely . <h> Memorial Day Weekend <p> Most people appeared to be practicing social distancing on the beach in Ocean City , Saturday , May 16 , 2020 . ( VERNON OGRODNEK / For The Press ) <p> VERNON OGRODNEK / For The Press <p> Expect plenty of time to enjoy the beach , boardwalk or the backyard , safely . Saturday will be the " wettest " day of the weekend . However , any rain will be brief . High pressure will then build in from Atlantic Canada , bringing plenty of sunshine and dry air . <p> Saturday will be the warmest day of the weekend , with 70s and a bit of humidity everywhere , even at the shore . The shores Sunday and Monday will be 65-70 degrees , with the mainland 70-75 . Keep the sweatshirt nearby , at the very least , you 'll need an extra layer at night . However , enjoy the rain free conditions in South Jersey . <h> Joe 's 7-Day Forecast <p> I 've been the Meteorologist at The Press since Fall 2017 . I 've spent my whole life in New Jersey , earning a Meteorology degree from Rutgers University . I 'm honored to be a 5 time N.J. Press Association award winner and a South Jersey " Top 40 Under 40 " . <h> Watch this discussion.Stop watching this discussion . <h> ( 0 ) comments <h> Welcome to the discussion . <p> Keep it Clean . @@31845082 <h> The seven rules of making a FF-FG-Green coalition work <p> If the Green Party enters government in the coming weeks , it will face a series of political , public health and economic challenges unmatched by any administration in the history of the State . <p> The party would also be entering government with an unprecedented combination of Fine Gael and Fianna F ? il , rivals for most of the last century , during which period each was dedicated to the electoral subjugation of the other . This novel alliance is going to take some getting used to . And both parties contain significant elements that are not just suspicious of the Greens , but wholly opposed to their worldview . <p> But for all these formidable obstacles , the leaders of the three parties have decided that there is a basis for a viable coalition . They have been backed by their TDs . There are obstacles to surmount for sure -- agreeing a final programme for government , gaining the endorsement of each party 's members -- but the parties are on course to form a government . <p> In an era that has seen nothing but coalition governments since 1989 , it is possible to see what works in a coalition , and what does n't <p> So how will it work for the Greens ? How will they maintain their identity and cohesion as the smallest partner ? Can they achieve their goals ? And can they avoid the electoral mangling that usually ( but not always ) awaits small parties in a post-coalition election ? <p> If the three-party coalition is put together ( with the possible support of a few external independents ) it will be unlike any government the State has ever seen . But in an era that has seen nothing but coalition governments since 1989 , it is possible to see what works in a coalition , and what does n't . <p> There are many veterans of coalitions that endured -- and of others that ended in disaster -- around to consult . So here are seven rules and principles that will make life in coalition not just bearable , but perhaps even productive . <h> 1 . Realise that electoral disaster is not inevitable <p> It is certainly true that many small parties have ended up being crucified by the voters after a coalition adventure . It happened to Labour following the 1994-97 coalition , and again after the 2011-16 coalition . It happened to the Greens after their last ( and only ) period in government in 2011 , when the party lost all its seats . <p> It happened to the Progressive Democrats ( PDs ) . It happened to the Democratic Left . It happened , you could argue , to the Independent Alliance at the February election , when none of its ministers ( along with another independent , Katherine Zappone ) retained their seats . <p> But it does n't have to be like that . In 2002 , the PDs doubled their D ? il seats from four to eight after five years in government with Fianna F ? il . A decade earlier , the party went from six seats to 10 after three years in a government led first by Charles Haughey , then by Albert Reynolds . " It was crisis after crisis after crisis , " says Stephen O'Byrnes , who was deputy government press secretary in that government . " But the PDs were associated with policy successes : privatisation , tax cuts , economic liberalisation . " <p> So as a matter of historical fact , it is possible for a small party to do okay out of government . In both cases , the PDs were able to claim credit for the successes of the government which were central to their political brand . <h> 2 . Get it in the programme for government <p> The programme for government agreed between the parties is the " Bible " of any coalition government , says Pat Rabbitte , former Labour leader and a minister in the Fine Gael-Labour coalition between 2011-14 . <p> " Whatever it is , if it 's in the programme for government , you have a good chance to getting it through . " <p> There is no guarantee that just because a policy is in the programme it will be implemented ; but there is virtually no chance if it is n't . In case of disagreement ( and there will be disagreements between the parties ; many of them ) they will revert to the programme . <p> It also gives new ministers the authority to insist their civil servants work to implement their policies . <h> 3 . Build trust <p> Easier said than done , but absolutely essential to the successful operation of a coalition government . " If you enter government with an agreement on policy in the programme for government and with the intention of trying to make it work , then it should work , " says a veteran of coalition in the 1990s and 2000s . <p> The parties need to trust that their partners are committed to the enterprise , and also have political needs . <p> Bertie Ahern was the master of running coalition governments , leading three of them from 1997-2008 . Whatever you may think of the performance of those administrations and the denouement that awaited following the financial crash of 2008 , he was twice re-elected and the administrations were mostly harmonious . <p> Ahern used to drive his ( Fianna F ? il ) ministers and staff mad with concessions to his coalition partners -- but he always knew they had to get something from the deal . " Even if we hated the PDs , we never went into a meeting with that attitude , " says one Fianna F ? il adviser at the time . <p> " Bertie never boxed himself into a corner he could n't get out of . There was a sort of brilliance to his vagueness . " <p> If the next government is to implement a Green policy , the party will have to convey to its partners how important those policies are to it ; but it will also have to appreciate that some of them are difficult for Fianna F ? il and Fine Gael. <h> 4 . Relationships are key at every level <p> Relationships between the parties operate at three related but distinct levels : staff , ministers and leaders . All three have to function effectively . The Fianna F ? il ministers and advisers got on like a house on fire with their Labour counterparts in the 1992-94 coalition , but the coalition still fell apart because the relationship between taoiseach Albert Reynolds and t ? naiste Dick Spring disintegrated . <p> The working relationships have to be scaffolded by structures -- regular meetings of advisers and political managers and a general " no surprises " rule are features of successful coalitions . <p> Key relationships : the party will need structures in place to function effectively . Photograph : Nick Bradshaw/The Irish Times <p> " Goodwill in the run-up , absolute respect and , once you 're in , it 's about proper structures to manage the relationship between the parties , " says Mandy Johnston , government press secretary to Ahern and adviser in his three coalitions . " You wo n't manage your partner . But you can manage your relationship with them . " <h> 5 . Build a strong centre of government <p> Effective coalition governments always have a strong centre . Spring learned from Labour 's miserable experience in the 1982-87 coalition and instituted a system of programme managers and advisers , attached to each minister and overseen by powerful figures at the centre of government , who managed the delivery of the administration 's programme . <p> " Greg Sparks and Sean Donlon commanded huge authority , " says a member of the 1994-97 government . The Economic Management Council of the Fine Gael-Labour coalition of 2011-16 commanded that government from the centre ; but when Joan Burton replaced Eamon Gilmore as Labour leader in 2014 , the relationship at the centre frayed , and so did the rest of the government . The personal and political relationship relationship between Ahern and PD leader Mary Harney at the centre of government was central to the stability of the Fianna F ? il- PD governments led by him . <h> 6 . Learn how to work the machine <p> Understanding and working the machine of government is a particular challenge for a small party with little or no experience of government . <p> Ministerial advisers are vital to this role . One minister recalls being alarmed when he found his special adviser in a meeting with his secretary general without his knowledge . He learned to value the relationship they had . <p> " A secretary-general can tell an adviser , ' the minister ca n't do that ' , " he says . " But he ca n't tell the minister that . " <h> 7 . Define a common purpose , and the Greens ' place in it <p> All governments need a purpose and each component needs to feel it has an important role in that . " If you do n't have that fundamental thing from the beginning , then everything is shaky , " says Johnston . " You 're in it together . " <p> The Progressive Democrats had tax cuts and economic liberalisation as part of the programme for economic recovery , and to progress that was the mission of the governments the party served in . In the first two governments , it worked ; it was when the PDs became indistinguishable from Fianna F ? il that the voters found them irrelevant . <p> The Greens will be targeted by their political opponents on the left , who are already accusing them of betraying the electorate 's desire for change <p> Labour never managed to distinguish itself sufficiently from Fine Gael , and paid the price . Some of that was Labour 's fault . But some of it was because Fine Gael never moved aside to give Labour policy wins . <p> For a shared mission to work , the parties have to communicate constantly , not just with the public , but with each other . The Greens will be particularly targeted by their political opponents on the left , who are already accusing them of betraying the electorate 's desire for change . <p> Some of its own members believe the same , though once in government , your voters are almost always more important than your members . The party will not appease its left-wing critics , but it can look to how the German Greens successfully " triangulated " -- refusing to be defined as either right or left , but rising above that division to co-operate with either as circumstances required . <p> " They wo n't get a guarantee that they 'll be okay at the end . They wo n't get everything they want , " says one coalition veteran . " But if their central message is : ' climate change is more important than anything else , and we 're going to do something about it ' , I think that 's the key for them . Announce your priorities and then achieve them . " <p> We reserve the right to remove any content at any time from this Community , including without limitation if it violates the Community Standards . @@31845190 <p> It was revealed in Bong Joon Ho 's 2013 feature film " Snowpiercer " that the titular train needed children in order to carry on its mission of lapping the globe in perpetual motion . They were cogs in the machine -- literal replacement parts -- as the train was already wearing down after only a few years of tearing through the frozen tundra that Earth had become . It was a bleak look at humanity 's chance at survival that was further enhanced by themes of social unrest between the classes that divided the train . <p> When Graeme Manson took on the role of showrunner for the television adaptation of this title , he wanted to keep a similar tone to the film -- " It was dark , but I also thought it was hilarious , " he tells Variety -- and he wanted to deepen the discussion around the class warfare , but he wanted to ground the story in both the human bond and a scientific base , which led to exploring trauma of a slightly different kind . <p> " Everybody feels like they did their piece to destroy the world and lose everyone and everything they ever knew , " Manson says of the characters in his version of " Snowpiercer . " " Most of the fears that are present in the show are things like migration , detention , immigration , privilege , and then climate change is just something that hangs over the whole show , and what hangs over every character is guilt . Everybody has that trauma within themselves . " <p> In order to better understand each character 's individual emotional pain and therefore journey , a different character narrates each episode , Manson notes . This allows individual episodes to give " a little closer look -- a sort-of internal look -- at what makes that character tick . " <p> When Manson came to the show , the characters of Andre Layton , a Tailie played by Daveed Diggs , and Melanie Cavill ( Jennifer Connolly ) , the voice of the train who claims to have a direct line to its maker , were already in place . The " Snowpiercer " TV series adaptation was first ordered to pilot at TNT in 2015 and to series in 2018 , undergoing a showrunner swap , director changes , network moves and a complete reshoot of the pilot along the way . Melanie calling upon Layton , a former detective , to solve a crime aboard the train became both an entry-point into and a cornerstone of the pilot for Manson because it was " a way to see the train for the first time through someone 's eyes who is also seeing much of it for the first time , " he says . <p> As Layton is plucked from his lower-class life in the back of the 1,001-car train , he literally walks through the cars that separate his people from the upper classes . <p> " One of the things that I love so much about the film is , when you were charging up the train with the Tailie rebels , you 'd never knew what was going to be on the next door . When we run five seasons , you can still open doors on surprising new cars . " <p> But Manson admits that while Layton 's investigation served as a way to set up this complicated new world , " there was never really a season-long murder mystery here . It was a way to get him out into the train . He has his own agenda , and that is one of resistance and revolution , and that 's the real story of the first season . We used the familiar to get into deeper territory . " <p> Layton 's travels within the train provide crucial information for him on how the train operates and the other passengers live . As Layton gets to know some of the first and second class passengers , the staff that serve them and Melanie herself , he , and the audience by extension , begins to " understand their fears and what drives them . " But more importantly , he begins to assess who can be used and who can be allies in the Tailies ' mission for a revolution to bring forth a better life . <p> " The revolution will be threatened , " Manson previews . " Conspiracy and secrets play heavily on the train , and misinformation , but what they are looking for is equal calories , fair representation . They 're attempting to write a constitution and we all know what that is . They 're attempting to revive democracy , and especially in these times , I think that is something important . It 's another one of those areas where the show rubs up against our current reality . "
