The predicted and simulated values are plotted against each other in Fig. 4b . Considering the high heterogeneity of the urban structure factors within the real UCP data and the derived scenario UCP data , we can conclude that our general regression form as in Eq . ( 3 ) holds not only for model-created urban structures , but also for real-world urban structures . In order to test the robustness of these results , we last perform an out-of-sample validation : we remove one simulation from the 21 samples , regress Eq . ( 3 ) , and obtain a prediction that is independent from its corresponding simulated value . Then , we repeat the procedure for each sample in the set ( leave-one-out cross-validation ) . Comparing the predicted and simulated values , we can see that the UHI intensities predicted by our approach show agreement with the simulated UHI intensities . Except for two values with a deviation of -0.21 ? K and 0.14 ? K , the rest of the predictions have an error within ? 0.1 ? K. <h> Discussion <p> The UHI effect can increase the frequency of extreme heat events , extend the duration of high temperatures , and narrow the time window for relief from high-heat exposure9,11,14 . This heat stress may deteriorate further when taking climate change and rapid ongoing urbanisation into account . Moreover , as the majority of world 's population already lives in cities , urban areas are expected to absorb the lion 's share of global population growth that is estimated to be 2.2 billion by the end of this century51 . This means that in the future many more people will be exposed to more frequent and intensified extreme heat events , not to mention demographic change and an increasing proportion of vulnerable elderly people . Therefore , urban development policies need to take the UHI effect into account21 and make proper use of effective ways to reduce excessive urban heat . <p> Achieving this goal requires more comprehensive understanding of how the UHI effect is influenced by key local- and regional-scale factors , such as urban canyon structure , building density , urban surface fraction , and urban form . A challenge in the study of cities is that many factors and characteristics vary among cities , most notably the background climate5 , thermal properties of the rural surface45 , city size41 , density44 , urban form52 , street geometry8,44 , and building material2,44 . Here , by employing simulated cities , we can keep the climate conditions constant and clearly define these factors , and thus investigate the UHI phenomenon for cities over almost two orders of magnitude . <p> We quantify the relationship between key urban factors and the UHI intensity , and propose a regression model to quantitatively estimate the UHI intensity based on detailed 3D urban structure data . Our results show that : firstly , given the same urban area or gross building volume , the UHI intensity is strongly influenced by the building density ( gross building volume per unit area , calculated as the product of total building plan area , and average building height within an urban area unit ) ; and secondly , increasing building density will lead to stronger UHI intensity . However , due to different effects of aspect ratio , increasing building plan area causes a more rapid increase in UHI intensity than adding vertical building height . Given knowledge about the coefficients , Eq . ( 3 ) can serve to quantify the effect of interventions on the city in question and to investigate scenarios of the urban development . <p> Our results confirm that increasing urban fraction and building height will enhance the UHI intensity , which is consistent with previous **26;950;TOOLONG . Although increasing building height means more shading effect and less heat storage within a street canyon during the day , it also leads to larger aspect ratios and lower night time cooling rates due to stronger trapping of outgoing radiation . The extent to which one of these two effects offsets another still requires further investigation . According to our results , increasing the building density through taller buildings leads to slower increase in UHI intensity , and the increase rate gets smaller for larger street canyon aspect ratio4 . On the other hand , based on numerical modelling , Marciotto et al . found a peak point of aspect ratio at 3.5 , beyond which the maximum UHI intensity will decrease with increasing aspect ratio25 . This is not a contradiction as in our work , most of the street canyons still have an aspect ratio &lt;3.5 even when the height of all buildings is doubled . However , it is also unrealistic to have a that large average aspect ratio within many grid cells at 1 ? km resolution . <p> Regarding the influence of urban form , our results show that the sprawling development will lead to a better thermal environment when considering the entire urban area . Stone et al . found that sprawled cities show a greater rate of increase in the frequency of annual extreme heat events33 . A reason for this difference could be their use of observational data acquired at weather stations that are often located near the airport instead of the city centre . Moreover , when the urban area and the gross building volume are controlled , the factors within the term D in Eq . ( 3 ) still interact with each other non-linearly . Under the premise that the street canyon geometry is homogeneous over all urban sites , the term D clearly indicates that more compact urban clusters will lead to higher UHI intensities . However , without this precondition the situation is more complex . Future work that links the quantity D to factors like urban fractality31,46,54 , urban **29;978;TOOLONG , anisometry31 , and intra-urban street canyon geometry will further our understanding of the influence of the urban form on the UHI effect . <p> Our results , to some extent , cross the scale hierarchy with regards to urban heat stress mitigation by aggregating the complex interactions of vegetation fraction and canyon geometry at the neighbourhood-scale grid cell ( in our case , at the scale of 1 ? km ) into an impact at the city scale . This means that city-scale UHI intensity can not simply be scaled up from that of the neighbourhood scale , as nearby neighbourhoods also influence each other . Since there is no single best design that meets all climate objectives1 , a quantitative assessment of the impact of different designs can help to balance between different objectives30,37,56,57,58 . However , it is beyond the scope of this paper to integrate our findings into a more holistic frame , since decision making on urban design is a very complex process that requires consideration of many other aspects . For example , a denser city can be preferable regarding energy efficiency but will lead to greater UHI intensity57 , a proper comparison requires quantitative assessment of both objectives . Even for the same objective of urban heat stress mitigation , it is difficult to clearly prefer one development design over another one before their detailed 3D urban structures are available , or at least some of the factors are fixed . The main reason is that the factors in Eq . ( 3 ) , in particular building height and street width , interact and impose limits on each other . Instead , our approach permits an assessment30,56,58 that takes the 3D urban structures of different urban development scenarios as inputs , and enables the comparison between these scenarios with regard to heat stress mitigation on the city scale . <p> Some limitations exist in this work and the application of our results . Firstly , besides urban form and factors related to street canyon geometry1 , weather conditions and rural surface characteristics44,45 play an important role in determining UHI intensities . To apply Eq . ( 3 ) to another city , one would need to derive the coefficient of the regression again , requiring 20 simulations . This hampers the fast application of our results , especially for those without expertise in running numerical climate simulations . Properly identifying a representative heat wave event and always using it as standard driving data could help to avoid unnecessary simulations . Secondly , with the coefficients known , applying Eq . ( 3 ) still requires detailed 3D urban structure data for the development scenarios under consideration . This data will become increasingly available with the rapid development of spatial information technology . Lastly , for simplification and to better separate the influences of the various factors , we excluded anthropogenic heat in this study . For Berlin , the influence of anthropogenic heat release on nocturnal UHI effect should be relatively small during summertime according to studies on other temperate cities45,59,60,61 . Moreover , during the night , anthropogenic heat release from cooling should be negligible as the majority of households do not use air conditioning . However , for cities or scenarios where cooling equipment is widely operated during hot summertime , UHI intensity can be increased by &gt;1 ? ? C ( refs. 62,63,64 ) . Further work on the influence of anthropogenic heat will be helpful for more accurate UHI prediction for cities , where cooling devices are widely used . <h> Methods <h> Climate model <p> The mesoscale non-hydrostatic climate model CCLM ( ref. 65 ) coupled with a multi-layer urban canopy model ( UCM ) , the DCEP ( ref. 34 ) , was used in this study . Previous work has shown that diurnal variation and magnitude of UHI can be well represented in CCLM/DCEP during summer months28,66 . <p> CCLM was developed from the operational weather forecast Local Model of the German Meteorological Service by the CLM-Community and has been the community model of the German climate research since 2005 . In the standard CCLM , cities are represented by a bulk-transfer scheme with modified soil and vegetation parameters . An urban scheme is necessary to represent important urban characteristics in terms of thermal properties and vertical effects of buildings28 . The DCEP scheme , based on the Building Effect Parametrization67 , accounts for the effects of buildings and streets configuration on the atmosphere . When coupled with CCLM , DCEP is only applied to the urban fraction of a mesoscale model grid cell , the remaining natural surface fraction is treated by the land surface scheme of CCLM . In DCEP , the urban surface is conceptualised as multiple series of identical street canyon elements that are characterised by canyon direction , street width , building height , and building width . Therefore , UCP required by DCEP for each urban grid cell are : urban surface fraction , canyon direction distribution , building height distribution , street width , and building width . <h> Model set-up and data analysis <p> We conducted a chain of three nested CCLM simulations with resolutions of 0.165 ? , 0.025 ? , and 0.009 ? , see coverage of each model domain in Supplementary Fig. 6b . The domain of the innermost simulation was centred at Berlin . A period of 1 week during a heat wave event was simulated28 . The coarsest simulation was driven by ERA-Interim reanalysis data with a spin-up time of 5 years . The remaining two nesting steps started 6 months and 12 days , respectively , before the analysed period . <p> The DCEP scheme is only applied in the finest simulations . To validate our model configuration , we conducted a reference run with UCP data derived from a 3D dataset of Berlin at 1 ? km resolution28 . Statistics of the model performance against observational data ( measured at six weather stations located in and near Berlin , see Supplementary Fig. 6b ) are shown in Supplementary Table 2 . In terms of mean error , mean absolute error , and root-mean-square error , the model satisfactorily reproduces the 2-m air temperature . <p> Configurations for the simulations with generated UCP data were the same with the reference run except that the external data , such as vegetation , orography , and soil parameters were made homogeneous based on the mean value of the finest domain . This minimises the effect of non-urban parameters on our results . <p> For each generated urban cluster , we define a non-urban boundary of approximately the same area by determining several layers of cells surrounding the urban area36 . The difference between average 2-m air temperatures of urban area and rural boundary area was taken as the canopy layer UHI intensity . <h> Urban growth model <p> We used a gravitational urban growth model39 to create realistic 3D urban canopy data . This model , based on the concept that growth is more likely to take place close to high densities , is capable of reproducing various attributes of real-world cities , such as the radial gradients of population density , radial gradients of urban fraction , and the power law between the population and city area . On a square grid , the probability of growth in cell i is given by ( pi=fracGMisum jne ivjdi , j-gamma ) , where ? is the main parameter , di , j is the Euclidean distance from cell i to j , vj is the value in cell j , Mi is a site-specific normalisation constant39,40 , and G is another parameter determining the overall rate of growth . Starting with a single v ? = ? 1 cell in the centre , the model is run iteratively incrementing the counts vi ? vi ? + ? 1 , if z ? &lt; ? pi , where z is a random number between 0 and 1 . The exponent ? controls the shape of the emerging urban clusters , i.e. , small ? lead to sprawled and radial symmetric structures , and large ? lead to compact forms with less radial symmetry . Consistent with ref. 39 , we explored ? ? 2.0 , 2.05 , ... , 2.7 , 2.75 and 1000 ? ? ? 1000 system size . <p> From the resulting 14,1758 clusters , for each ? value we first select one cluster with an area of approximate 2000 cells ( as we put these clusters in the climate model domain with 1 ? km2 resolution , its area corresponds to 2000 ? km2 ) . The corresponding gross building volume increases with ? . We name these clusters set 1 , and took the cluster for ? ? = ? 2.5 in set 1 as reference cluster Cref . Similarly , we select one cluster for each ? value that has approximately the same gross building value as Cref . The corresponding cluster areas decrease with ? . We name these clusters set 2 . At last , another nine clusters emerging from the same growth sequence ( realisation ) as Cref are selected . Together with Cref , they make up set 3 . In addition , ten clusters from different ? values are selected according to the criterion that they are close to Cref in terms of gross building volume and size . They constitute set 4 . See Supplementary Fig. 1 for the cross plot of size versus gross building volume of all selected clusters and some of them depicted . <h> 3D UCP data <p> In order to make use of the gravitational urban growth model output , the grid value vi in pixel i was taken as the floor count of the building in this pixel . The system was aggregated into to a coarser domain of 200 ? ? ? 200 , thus each coarse pixel consists of 25 finer pixels with values v1 , v2 , . . . , v25 . Then the urban fraction fu of this coarse pixel was calculated as ( fracN ( vi , &gt; , 0 ) 25 ) , where N(*) is a function that counts the number of considered values that match the criterion of it . Only coarse pixels with urban fraction no &lt;20% were taken as urban cells68 , in the end we got a 200 ? ? ? 200 urban/non-urban matrix for each output . For some outputs from large ? values , the v values of pixels near the centre become very large after many interations . In order to have more realistic city centres , we applied a threshold of 30 for maximum average number of building storeys on each coarse pixel and rescaled the building height distribution as follow . If ( barv=fracsum viN ( vi , &gt; , 0 ) &gt; 30 ) , ( vi=frac30vibarv ) , thus the average building height ( barv ) for all coarse pixels will not exceed 30 storeys . Then for each coarse pixel marked as urban cell , we calculated the building height distribution fh1 , fh2 , . . . , fhj following ( frmhi=fracN ( vi , = , i ) ... &gt; , 0 ) ) , where fhi denotes the share of buildings with height of i storeys , and j is the maximum value of the original 1000 ? ? ? 1000 lattice . <p> We applied the CCA algorithm69 on the aggregated urban/non-urban matrix to assign all urban pixels into clusters . In this study , we only focus on the central , largest cluster of each output . In addition , only the central clusters with &gt;200 pixels , which do not touch any edge of the coarse domain were considered . <p> For each coarser grid cell , the proportion of urban surface occupied by building footprints was calculated28 as ( frmb=fracWrmbY , + ... where Wb and Y are building width and street width , respectively . The building volume w for each grid was calculated according to <p> where Agrd is the area of the grid cell ( 1 ? ? ? 1 ? km2 throughout all the simulations ) , fu is urban fraction measured as urban surface fraction , ( barv ) is the aforementioned average building height measured by the number of storeys , and Hf is the floor height ( we assume constant floor height of 3 ? m for all buildings to further simplify conditions in this study ) , see the notation in Supplementary Table 3 . We take the number of pixels of the considered cluster as the urban size A , and the sum of the building volume covered by the cluster as the gross building volume , namely ( S = sum wi ) . <p> For other parameters required by the DCEP scheme , such as street direction distribution , street width , and building width28 , we first assumed they are distributed homogeneously within the urban area in order not to introduce further variability . The fraction for each direction ( -45 ? , 0 ? , 45 ? , and 90 ? to the north clockwise ) in each pixel is 25% . For street width Y and building width Wb , 20 ? m and 15 ? m are taken , respectively . Based on the selected clusters , 50 UCP datasets are created . <p> We create additional 42 UCP datasets that feature ten spatial patterns ( see Supplementary Fig. 3 and Table 1 for examples of each pattern ) , which are named set 5 . For these clusters , we chose a street canyon width of 15 ? m and building width of 20 ? m . We take a different street canyon width compared to sets 1 -- 4 , since in set 5 some of the clusters are rather small and as smaller canyon width leads to stronger UHI intensities , we have a better signal to noise ratio . <p> To study how the street canyon width influences the parameters a1 , a2 , a3 in Eq . ( 1 ) , we pick five UCP datasets from set 1 and another five from set 3 to create additional UCP data . Based on each of these UCP datasets , we then create four new UCP datasets by only changing the street canyon width to 10 ? m , 15 ? m , 25 ? m and 30 ? m , respectively , and changing the building width accordingly to keep the fraction of building plan area unchanged . Then for each street width in 10 , 15 , 20 , 25 , 30 m , we get ten simulations and fit the results with Eq . ( 1 ) . Comparing resulting a1 , a2 , a3 , we are able to study the influence of the street width . These modified UCP datasets are together named set 6 . <p> The parameters taken for different UCP datasets can be found in Supplementary Table 4 . <h> UCP data from different urbanisation scenarios of Berlin <p> To illustrate how our findings can be used in for real-world cities , we create a series of UCP data based on different hypothetical urbanisation scenarios for Berlin . This is done by modifying the real UCP data taken for the reference run . Assuming that the change of living space only happens in vertical direction , we increased ( or decreased ) the average building height proportionally by -50% , -25% , +25% , +50% , and +100% . Thus , we get five UCP scenarios with a gross building volume increment of -50% , -25% , 25% , 50% , and 100% relative to the real UCP data . <p> Similarly , we can also allocate the change by altering the urban fraction . For the scenarios of decreasing gross building volume by 50% and 25% , we simply decrease the urban fraction of each grid cell by 50% and 25% . However , for increasing gross building volume scenarios , we decrease the vegetation surface of each grid cell by the same percentages to get three scenarios with gross building volume increased by 25% , 50% , and 100% . Similar method has been used by Schubert and Grossman-Clarke28 . <p> It has to be noted that both vertical changes and horizontal changes are constrained within already urbanised grid cells , that is , without changing the shape of the urban cluster . In the third scenario the change of gross building volume is achieved by modifying the extent of the urban cluster . This is implemented by randomly adding or removing urban grid cells . For decreased gross building volume scenarios , we simply repeated the process of randomly removing an urban grid cell from the edge of the cluster . For increased gross building scenarios , the following steps are repeated until the gross building volume of the expanded urban cluster approximately agrees with the desired size . Step 1 : randomly pick a grid cell from the urban cluster ; step 2 : randomly select a non-urban grid cell that is adjacent to an urban grid cell ; and step 3 : replace this non-urban cell with the urban cell selected by step 1 . At the end , we get ten scenario UCP datasets with gross building volume changed by -50% , -25% , -10% , +10% , +25% , +40% , +50% , +60% , +75% , and 100% respectively , <h> Code availability <p> The source code of the COSMO-CLM model is available from the CLM-Community ( clm-community.eu ) after registration . We will never share your email address with third parties without your permission . By signing in , you are indicating that you accept our Terms of Service and Privacy Statement . <p> Earlier today the winners of the 2020 Kavli Prize for Nanoscience were announced . Professor Harald Rose of Universit ? t Ulm and Technical University of Darmstadt , Professor Maximilian Haider of CEOS GmbH , Professor Knut Urban of Forschungszentrum J ? lich and Professor Ondrej L Krivanek of Nion Co. have been awarded the $1 million prize for the refinement and application of aberration-correcting lenses in nanoscale microscopy that has since enabled researchers to observe individual atoms of materials . I chatted to two of the four winners , Professor Maximilian Haider and Professor Knut Urban , to find out about the areas of science they are most excited to see benefiting from their prize-winning development , research culture , role models , and so much more . <p> Professor Maximilian Haider and Professor Knut Urban , two of the four winners of the 2020 Kavli ... + Prize for Nanoscience <p> Professor Haider , Professor Urban , thank you for taking the time to answer my questions today . I was wondering whether we could talk about your successes , and any potential failures you encountered along the way . When we hear about scientific discoveries , it is easy to imagine that the researchers behind these discoveries know exactly what they are looking for . Was this the case for you ? Tell me about your journey from the lab bench to the commercial adoption of your development . What role did collaboration with other researchers and with industry played in it ? <p> MH : Our case is unusual because the performance of electron microscopes reached a certain limit just above the 1 ? ngstrom barrier , and all attempts to circumvent this resolution limit did not work properly . Objects being observed could not withstand the high energy if a shorter wavelength was used . Many images had to be acquired to dig into the smaller details of materials by focus reconstruction . In the 1980s and 1990s , materials scientists waited impatiently to find a way to overcome the resolution barrier . Suddenly the aberration correction worked and opened up a new view into the atomic world of solid objects . I think that close cooperation between research and industry is beneficial for all , but what counts much more is the collaboration and understanding of the needs of researchers and respect for each other . A business strategy with the highest priority on making profit could be counterproductive for the scientific community . <p> KU : This can only be determined on a case-by-case basis . From our point of view , there are three things : Industry 's primary task is to design a good product , market it well and earn money with it . For cost reasons , Industry can not engage in basic research , or very risky research and development . This is down to the nature of completely new research ; the really innovative , that one can not from the outset say whether a research project will be successful or not . In order to achieve something really new , as in our case , one must also be able to take expensive wrong turns , be able to make mistakes and still be able to try out apparently hopeless paths . It is therefore not surprising that industry has not shown any interest in our research project . We had to proceed with the development of the aberration corrected electron microscopy alone . Funding agencies worldwide were not willing to finance this work . The reason for this was that , over many decades , people had tried in vain to find a technical solution for the aberration correction of electron lenses . It took a long time to convince the Volkswagen Foundation in Germany that our plans made sense . We then drove the development to the prototype ; a microscope that you could really work with . Even after we had achieved sensational research results with it , industry was very skeptical as to whether they would ever be able to make money with it . Any really new thing is also a commercial risk . One thing is for sure : It would not have been possible to make this development with our aberration-corrected electron microscopy in direct cooperation with industry , owing to the risks of novel research . Having proven its worth , this has now changed , and Industry has also made a lot of money with this invention . <p> The 2020 Kavli Prize for Nanoscience is just one of many prizes that your international , cross-disciplinary team of researchers has won . How much do you think your work has benefitted from a research culture that favors international collaboration , and do you think the same opportunities are available to researchers today , in the face of limited funding and issues such as Brexit . <p> MH : Our initial collaboration in Germany was actually the basis for our success . We were also driven by a race to the best resolution microscopy . This race gave us a kick to be better . However , fairness and acceptance of good results of other scientists should not be forgotten . I assume and I hope opportunities for a beneficial collaboration do always exist , as long as we are working in an open-minded environment , free from restrictions by the government or other powerful bodies . Hence , any restriction of traveling , meeting other labs or open discussions would reduce the productivity of money invested in research . In Europe , we have various networks in science that . Many British scientists benefited from these funded activities . It is very bad that British scientists wo n't have the same access to all the well-equipped laboratories in Europe as they had before Brexit . <p> KU : From my experience , I know that there are many scientists who do not trust their colleagues , and therefore prefer to do their research alone . Nevertheless , there are many funded research projects in Europe and in other industrialized countries that can only be obtained if an interdisciplinary team can be offered . This has significantly promoted the culture of interdisciplinary research . In my field , materials research , I see that the important papers in Science or Nature Group journals are often written by large teams . Each team brings its own expertise to the project . Again , I think that pressure from funding agencies is increasingly leading to the formation of larger interdisciplinary teams . <p> The potential for this is far from exhausted . I believe that the future of research , especially in large and well-funded projects , lies with larger interdisciplinary groups . I am confident that the attitude of individual researchers to collaboration will also change over time . It was clear from the outset of our project that a group of at least three would be funded . A pure device-development project of my two colleagues would not have been accepted . The requirement that a materials scientist had to be involved was clear from the outset . The focus had to be on application . <p> As you can see , we are awarded the prize not only for the development of the device , but also for its application . Since our introduction of aberration-corrected electron optics into electron microscopy , the electron optics industry has experienced a boom with great commercial success . The grouping of a theoretical physicist , an experimental electron optics specialist and a materials scientist has been successful , as can be seen . <p> With regard to current research culture , I see a tendency , on a European level above all , to want to force research into early cooperation with industry . This stems from a deep mistrust of the funding bureaucracy towards scientific research and the pressure from industry . When I was still President of the German Physical Society , I pointed out time and again that there is no investigation whatsoever into the extent to which this forced industry-oriented policy is really successful . Remember , in our case industry was not interested at all . Yet today they are making big money with it . <p> Regarding politics , Brexit is a difficult problem . Of course , I am against it . There is one point that is rarely mentioned . We , as people born in war , still remember the impactful pictures of Europe at war . For me , to live and work together in Europe was a goal of this and future generations . People have short memories when it comes to conflict . Germany , France and England would have formed a good team . The idealistic aspect of people is far more important to me than the economic aspect , which is absolutely secondary - just like the question of refugees . A tragedy . <p> Your developments in the area of nanomicroscopy and imaging have paved the way for many advances in research . My own research benefits greatly from the observational and analytical power that electron microscope has allowed me . What is your favorite area of novel research that has come about because of aberration-corrected electron microscopy and better nanoscale imaging and analysis in general ? <p> MH : For me , the most exciting developments are those that help us to carry out research against climate change . Our development of these new instruments supports this research by helping researchers have a look inside nanomaterials , and to understand the structure and function of such tiny objects . For example , electron microscopy can be used to understand the mode of action of solar cells and to optimize their efficiency , as well as find the best way to store the produced power in batteries . In both cases , it is essential to understand the processes at the atomic level . <p> KU : The study of materials and even of devices in atomic dimensions is an old dream of materials research . Measuring parameters at atomic dimensions that determine macroscopic behavior is perhaps the most comprehensive change that this new electron microscopy has made possible . We are still in the early stages , and there is still a lot of potential . One area that currently benefits directly from aberration-corrected electron microscopy is battery research . Lithium can be seen , imaged and measured with these new microscopes . Research into oxide materials has also received a major boost , because the corrected microscopes allow oxygen to be seen for the first time . The electron-optical industry is also a field that has naturally experienced a huge upswing . This should not be forgotten . Before our invention , around 1990 , this industry was in a difficult phase of stagnation and a number of companies left . Today business is booming . <p> This year , the three Kavli Prizes have been awarded to seven researchers that happen to be men . This is rare for the Kavli Prize , who have not had all-male Laureates in a decade . The Kavli Prize committee have from the outset taken many steps to ensure fairness in their selection process , which I think is evident in the diversity of their Laureates . There are now many initiatives in place that are attempting to recruit and retain a wider range of people into research . To that end , what do you think we should do to ensure that we retain a representative research workforce in terms of gender , ethnicity , socio-economic background , and what initiatives do you think are working well to level the playing field ? <p> MH : I am happy that you noticed this year 's unbalanced group of awardees . However , I assume this happened by coincidence and not by intention . What can we do to have a more representative diversity of gender , ethnicity , socioeconomic background and so on ? I think the only way is to be open to all kinds of people , and to support them independent of gender , ethnicity , or birth . We are the people who have achieved a certain level of education and we can give this knowledge we obtained to the next generation . Although our abilities and possibilities are limited , we can always act as human exemplars of how to cooperate and to interact with each other . <p> KU : I have worked in various positions in recent years to promote the integration of women into physics research . I think that we are making progress in Germany . After all , almost half of the PhD students in Germany in physics are women . However , most of them still decide to pursue a non-academic career or choose to start a family . In physics , the proportion of women in professorships is clearly far too small . Physics is simply not an attractive enough profession to retain a wider range of researchers . This needs to be worked on . After all , it is much easier to combine work and family life in Germany today - almost all universities and research centers offer childcare , which is very well received by parents . <p> Role models and mentors play a big part in retaining people within the research profession . Would you like to take the opportunity to tell us who your role models are , and shine a light on a researcher that you admire ? <p> MH : I left school at the age of 14 and started an apprenticeship as an optician , so I missed some opportunities at school to get a wider education . However , I had the drive to work hard to achieve the goals I set myself , and I learned to concentrate on the next step , rather than dream about something far in the future . Step by step , I achieved the closest targets and , hence , in the long run I felt that this ambiguous and challenging project of a working aberration corrector could also successfully be achieved . In this long period of working with many various people - men , women , engineers , scientists and many others - I learned a lot from all of these colleagues . I really admired some of them , and while working with them they partly became an idol . By " partly " , I mean that I was fascinated by the way they were thinking or working . Sometimes people are very good scientists but at the same time they show strange behaviors against people from other parts of the world . I admire the positive traits of many people I have worked with in my career , and do not follow or propagate any unfairness I see in this profession . <p> KU : This is an interesting question , not least because I have given it little thought so far . I would say quite unconventionally , and I wrote this in my autobiography for the Kavli Foundation , that the most important role model is my father . I think I owe a lot to him ; my understanding of other parts of culture , art , and music . In our family , a culture of knowledge and discussion was cultivated , which has guided me throughout my life . A great advantage for my profession as a physicist . As far as my later teachers are concerned , I learned a lot from them , but I often derived from these personalities what I did not want to do , or confirmation that I did not want to do things the way they wanted to do it . I know that I am not the only one who has had such experiences . Among my colleagues and friends , their qualities that are especially important to me are their skills and at the same time their modesty . They are all thoughtful types . They are all open to discussion , and always question their own views . This is a quality that I consider to be particularly important in an environment that is governed above all by opinions . Most people form these opinions at some point and then they do n't change them . What I have learned over all these years is - typical for a scientist - the self-critical approach to one 's own views and the need to learn to be humble at all times . <p> Professor Haider , Professor Urban , thank you so much for taking the time to share your views . It has been a pleasure to hear more from you both , and congratulations again on winning the 2020 Kavli Prize for Nanoscience . <p> The world around us is made of ' stuff . Without them , we 'd have to move from a 21st-century lifestyle back to the 19th century . <p> Biden 's decision to put Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez in charge of formulating his energy policy is like putting two vegans in charge of overseeing all U.S. meat production . <p> The Keystone XL pipeline needs State Department approval because it crosses into the U.S. from Canada . Six comprehensive reviews by the department over a decade found Keystone XL could be built and operated in an environmentally safe manner . State environmental reviews along the route came to the same conclusion . <p> A State Department study commissioned during the Obama administration determined the pipeline would create 3,200 temporary construction jobs directly , 42,000 additional jobs indirectly , and generate over $2 billion in wages and hundreds of millions of dollars in property taxes . It would boost the U.S. gross domestic project by an estimated $3.4 billion annually . <p> Keystone XL should have begun construction in 2011 . The same Obama State Department study concluded it would not contribute significantly to climate change . And remember , the Obama administration praised itself for doing the most ever to combat climate change . One could say " the science is settled . " <p> Obama should have trusted the advice of his own administration 's experts and given the pipeline the green light , but it was an election year . Mitt Romney , the Republican presidential nominee , was within two points of Obama in the polls . Romney had enthusiastically supported the Keystone XL pipeline and Obama needed the progressive base , so the president punted . <p> Obama did n't cancel the project altogether . Clearly , he understood Keystone XL 's economic benefits . But a delay bought him valuable time leading up to his reelection bid . After winning reelection in 2012 , Obama should have moved the project forward for the good of the nation . Instead , he delayed another four years . <p> Finally , in 2016 Obama denied all the necessary government permits for Keystone XL , citing " climate change , " in direct contradiction of his own State Department 's conclusion . The economic benefits ( jobs , tax revenue ) and national security benefits ( energy independence ) no longer mattered . Obama was cementing his legacy as a green president . <p> However , Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump tweeted : " If I am elected President I will immediately approve the Keystone XL pipeline . No impact on environment &amp; lots of jobs for U.S. " And true to his word , President Trump signed an executive order five days after his inauguration allowing the Keystone XL pipeline to cross into the U.S. from Canada . <p> Keystone XL is now under construction , but its political baggage endures . Radical environmentalists have proclaimed it a symbol of their opposition to fossil fuels . And now Biden has bowed to their irrational demand to stop construction of the pipeline . <p> Would President Biden tear down the pipeline 's construction at taxpayers ' expense ? Our close ally Canada would not appreciate that . And Canada is not going to stop producing oil . <p> So what would Biden accomplish by blocking Keystone XL ? <p> Instead of sending the oil to the U.S. through the Keystone XL pipeline , Canada could continue sending oil here via truck and rail -- a more dangerous and costly shipping method than pipelines . Canada could also ship more oil to China or elsewhere in Asia via oil tankers -- again , a more costly and dangerous mode of transportation . <p> Losing our northern neighbor 's reliable , inexpensive oil to China or elsewhere in Asia would be a foreign policy nightmare , but if Biden wants to continue the Obama-Biden tradition , foreign policy nightmares are to be expected . <p> And if we wind up importing more oil from the Middle East to make up for the loss of the Keystone XL pipeline -- and losses in domestic oil production created by other Biden policies -- that will worsen greenhouse gas emissions and put our national security in the hands of unstable regimes not always friendly to the U.S. <p> One thing is for sure : stopping the Keystone XL pipeline will not magically end our use of oil and other fossil fuels . <p> Supporting Keystone XL was a winning issue for Trump in 2016 and it can be again this year . His policies that have brought our country more jobs , a stronger foreign policy , a stronger economy , greater national security and energy independence have all made America great again . <p> Biden is foolish to attempt to make Keystone XL a political issue . America needs energy . America needs jobs . Our nation does n't need more Obama-Biden posturing and holding up vital energy projects to create a phony green legacy that will hurt the American people .

@@31866195 <h> Is it okay to have children in a time of climate chaos ? <p> ' There 's a scientific consensus that the lives of children are going to be very difficult , ' US Democratic Party politician Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said . <p> Climate change is bringing about a radical realignment in our moral thinking . If we have just a few years to save the planet , then reducing carbon emissions becomes the global priority number one . <p> This has implications for governments and businesses in strategic decisions , but also for individuals in their most intimate and personal choices . Should you eat steak ? Should you drive a car ? Should you use airlines ? Added to these questions , more people are asking : Should you have children ? <p> When Josephine Ferorelli and Meghan Kallman first met at a concert in 2014 they discovered they were separately grappling with this dilemma . Both aged 30 at the time , the Chicago-based writer and Rhode Island sociologist decided to set up Conceivable Future -- a network for people feeling conflicted about starting a family against the backdrop of impending climate chaos . <p> It has since collected dozens of testimonies from across the world . <p> " My partner and I have taken the decision that unless global attitudes change entirely ( which does n't seem plausible within our lifetime ) , it would be inconceivable for us to bring children into the world , " writes one Irish woman ( 37 ) on the site . <p> " It has sometimes been difficult to deny the natural urges that comes to approaching this age in life . Every time I do , I just take a stroll along the plastic covered beaches or a walk through what 's left of the forests here in Ireland . How much more damage do we have to cause for people to come to the same realisation ? " <p> The sentiment is spreading . " <p> With Conceivable Future , you say you 're inviting people to join a " highly personal and deeply political conversation " . Is part of your motivation to help people who may feel isolated in deliberating about these issues ? <p> JF&amp;MK : " Yes , a major reason that we founded Conceivable Future was because we recognised that the climate crisis -- as we 've been taught to think of it -- is an isolating and alienating issue . People were experiencing so much individually . Our generation has taken up the burden of shame that should belong to those that profit from fossil fuels , and this shame has created a social taboo against speaking of the real future , and how we imagine ourselves in it . <p> Meghan Kallman and Josephine Ferorelli set up Conceivable Future after meeting at a concert in 2014 <p> " Many people who we 've spoken with felt as though they were treated as crazy for thinking through what climate change meant for their reproductive lives . Aside from the general relief many participants express at finding others who share their concerns , the main narrative , whether people are leaning toward childbearing or not , is that the future is terrifyingly uncertain , and that most of what we were raised to believe about how our lives would be is proving untrue or inadequate , and that the scale of the crisis is so vast that it makes it hard to feel that even the biggest life decisions are important . <p> " Many participants have said that they fear if they do n't have children they wo n't have any children in their lives , that they 'll become more isolated . @@31867086 <h> Washington state aims to regulate water temperature at federal dams , wading into controversy <p> The Columbia is the great river of the West , winding from the north to meet its largest tributary , the Snake in Eastern Washington , then dividing the states of Oregon and Washington on its push to the sea . Big and powerful , its wild energy has been tamed to engineered stair steps controlled by locks and dams . <p> But what has worked well for navigation and carbon-free hydropower production has been a killer for salmon , as its now-lazy reservoirs heat up in summer . When the water gets hot enough for long enough , salmon stop migrating , and even die of stress and disease . <p> Today Columbia and Snake River salmon , and orcas that depend on them , are at risk of extinction . And Washington state regulators are taking a new regulatory role to chill fish-killing hot water at four dams in the lower Columbia , and four in the lower Snake . <p> Regulators also have a new tool to work with , in a just-published analysis of heat pollution in the river by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency ( EPA ) , open to public comment until July 21 . <p> Temperatures always have spiked in the rivers at times in summer , even before the dams . But today , the effects of the dams combined with the cumulative effects of climate change , push temperatures in the Columbia and lower Snake rivers over the state maximum temperature of 68 degrees for weeks on end , the EPA found . <p> Impacts vary by dam location , and time of year . In general , temperatures are highest in August , and the lower down in the Columbia Basin the dam , the bigger the problem . John Day Dam , east of The Dalles , was the biggest offender in the EPA 's analysis , with the biggest cumulative temperature impact . <p> Advertising <p> But the lower Snake River heats up , too : At Ice Harbor Dam , temperatures exceeded the state standard on average in August 100% of the time . <p> The EPA findings are stoking long-simmering controversy in the region over dam removal on the lower Snake River . Using a mathematical model to assess the temperature impacts under varying conditions , the EPA estimated a free-flowing lower Snake River would be within state temperature limits , even in August . <p> The Columbia and Snake are essential sources of chinook salmon for southern resident orcas , providing food at a hungry time of year before the orcas make their way to their summer feeding grounds in the Salish Sea , the transboundary waters between the U.S. and Canada , and Puget Sound . <p> Brett VandenHeuvel , executive director at Columbia Riverkeeper , said only dam removal on the lower Snake can save orcas and salmon from extinction . " We are beyond tinkering at the edges , " he said . <p> The nonprofit and other conservation and fishing groups initiated litigation that ultimately led to publication of the EPA 's analysis , and opened the door for the state Department of Ecology to take a new regulatory role for the state at eight federal dams , four on the lower Columbia and four on the lower Snake . <p> This is the first time Washington has engaged its authority to regulate water-quality standards , including temperature , at federal dams -- though it already does so at nonfederal dams all over the state . There are many steps ahead in the process , including public review , and rights to appeal . <p> Advertising <p> Temperature is not a new problem on the Columbia and Snake . Releases of cold water from big storage dams upstream and infrastructure built at several dams already are used to help cool water temperatures in summer . But the cooling effects are soon swamped by hot water downstream . <p> So much heat is baked into the river by climate change that on the lower Columbia , the temperature standard could not be met at three of the four dams in August even in an entirely free flowing river , the EPA found . <p> That just shows the state standard is unachievable , some said -- particularly with summer water temperatures already over the limit before the Columbia and Snake even cross the borders from B.C. and Idaho into Washington . " We and our members acknowledge that temperature is a really serious issue , " said Kurt Miller , executive director of Northwest River Partners , which represents industrial river users and utilities . <p> " But we are concerned the plan that eventually emerges from this could be really costly for electricity customers across the region , without being able to achieve the goal , " Miller said . " That would be a bad outcome . " <p> It 's too early for that kind of talk , state regulators say . <p> " Everyone wants to jump to ' Oh this is impossible , ' " said Vince McGowan , water quality program manager for Ecology , which will work with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers , which operates the dams , to implement state temperature standards . The Corps has two years to generate temperature management plans for the dams . A whole suite of actions could be taken to cool the rivers , up to and including dam removal . <p> " This is just the beginning , we are going to have that opportunity to talk about what can happen and what is feasible , " McGowan said . <p> " We are on a path where we can have those conversations with dam operators working with us on how they are going to meet our temperature standards , " McGowan said . " Which are just critical for protecting and restoring salmon runs . " <h> STRUGGLING FISH <p> Temperature is only one of the problems facing Columbia and Snake salmon -- but when the problem is severe and sustained , hot water is a major threat to survival for fish already struggling to hang on . <p> More than a dozen runs of salmon and steelhead are listed as threatened and endangered in the Columbia and Snake rivers . Despite spending billions of dollars to save Columbia Basin salmon , since the first listing in 1991 not a single salmon run has recovered . Now another species is at risk : the southern resident orcas , down to a population of just 72 , in part because they can not reliably get enough Chinook salmon , their preferred food , to eat . <p> The orcas take fish out of a vast hunting range . But the Columbia and Snake are such important food sources some scientists believe the orcas can not beat extinction without dam removal on the lower Snake to boost runs in the river , once the source of 40% of all Columbia Basin spring and summer Chinook . " I really believe if they do n't take the lower Snake dams out we are not going to recover the whales , " said Sam Wasser , director of the Center for Conservation Biology at the University of Washington , who has led a multiyear study of nutritional stress in the southern resident orcas based on analyzing hormones in the whales ' scat . <p> The EPA documented a warming trend in the Columbia and Snake rivers since 1960 of 1.5 degrees Celsius , or 2.75 degrees Fahrenheit , plus or minus half a degree . Salmon are cold-water animals and even slightly elevated temperatures for extended periods can kill them . The problem is predicted to get worse , because of rising air temperatures and changing weather , snowpack and runoff patterns . How much worse depends on how much people pollute and warm the atmosphere with carbon emissions , primarily by burning fossil fuels . <p> Advertising <p> It 's a world that was n't thought of back when the dams were built -- most of them before Washington adopted its temperature standard under the Clean Water Act . <h> SPECTACULAR RIVER <p> Until the dam-building era began in earnest in the early 1930s , the wild Columbia was a spectacular slasher of a river , sticklebacked with bone crushing rock , swirling with sucking whirlpools , foaming with rapids , chutes and drops , and rainbowed with spray as it smashed its way through rock walls in a 1,290-mile run from B.C. to the Pacific . <p> Home to every species of salmon and steelhead , the river was alive in every season of the year and thronged with salmon 10 to 16 million strong , the wealth of native people living from its abundance . <p> But the river is now also a unique source for hydropower , with a steep drop draining the snowmelt from mountain ranges across the 259,000-square-mile Columbia River basin . Eventually 281 larger dams were built throughout the basin , home to 40% of the hydropower capacity of the entire nation , juicing power lines all over the West . <p> But dams also alter rivers in many ways that on the Columbia and lower Snake are combining with climate change to heat the river by an order of magnitude more than any other cause , the EPA found . The dams create a backwater effect that extends upstream , in large impoundments of water . That also slows water travel times , to 7 to 15 times longer between upstream and downstream points in the river today than under free flowing conditions in the Columbia , and 8 to 13 times longer on the lower Snake , the EPA reported . <p> The channel widths of the river also are wider in reservoirs that act as slow-moving heat sinks . The run-of-river dams on the main-stem Columbia and lower Snake also do n't have the deep , cold water reserves of the big storage dams upstream , or the cooling freshets of free flow . <p> The Snake was a hot river in summer even before the dams , notes Matt Rabe , director of public affairs for the Corps ' Northwestern Region . But the dams and climate change have combined to create a much bigger temperature problem for fish over many more days in summer , despite what the Corps has already done to attack the problem . <p> " Obviously , " Rabe said , " temperature is something everyone has had their eye on for a long time . " <p> Lynda V. Mapes : 206-464-2515 or lmapes@seattletimes.com ; on Twitter : @LyndaVMapes.Lynda specializes in coverage of the environment , natural history , and Native American tribes .

I think they made a lot of allowances for his personality because he was such a great musician . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ottawa guitarist Roddy Ellias recalled that O&amp;rsquo ; Connor could sing improvised jazz solos that sounded exactly like what he would play on his horn . &amp;ldquo ; He ingrained that in me , so that was my ideal &amp;mdash ; try to play what you&amp;rsquo ; re singing inside , &amp;rdquo ; Ellias said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; About a dozen years ago , when Ottawa pianist Steve Boudreau was in his late 20s and O&amp;rsquo ; Connor was in his late 70s , the two musicians played every Sunday afternoon at Chez Lucien for a year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; He would have a genuine conversation on any topic with anybody who cared to sit down and say hi , &amp;rdquo ; Boudreau remembered . &amp;ldquo ; His interest in other people and the world in general made a lasting impression on me. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;div&gt;Boudreau , who described O'Connor 's playing as " effortless , playful and exciting , " added : " Every time I saw Hugh he was having a good time , whether he was on the clock or not . I aspire to that kind of life . " &lt;/div&gt; &lt;p&gt; O&amp;rsquo ; Connor was predeceased by his wife , Marion , and three of his five children , said Sharon O&amp;rsquo ; Connor . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **25;2468;TOOLONG " **32;2495;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; Peter HumThu , 23 Apr 2020 13:32:29 **45;2529;TOOLONG ... Arts'What other jazz orchestra does that ? ' : Adonis Rose comes to Ottawa to champion the music of New Orleanshttp : **33;2576;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;2611;TOOLONG ... title= " Adonis Rose , Artistic Director of New Orleans Jazz Orchestra . " alt= " Adonis Rose , Artistic Director of New Orleans Jazz Orchestra . " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;2647;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1563989 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The rhythms of New Orleans flow through drummer Adonis Rose&amp;rsquo ; s veins. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The sashaying grooves of the birthplace of jazz are in Rose&amp;rsquo ; s blood , as surely as they were passed down from his father , drummer Vernon Severin , who in turn had a drummer , Wilfred Severin , as his father . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Rose , who is in his mid-40s , took up a prime role as a musical leader in his hometown a few years ago . After playing in the New Orleans Jazz Orchestra for 15 years , Rose in 2017 became the 18-piece big band&amp;rsquo ; s artistic director . He&amp;rsquo ; ll be at the helm ( and behind his drum kit ) when NOJO plays the Shenkman Arts Centre in Orl&amp;eacute ; ans on Tuesday , presenting a concert focused on the music of the great New Orleans composer Allen Toussaint. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Below , Rose discusses the cultural mission of NOJO and what makes it unique . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Q : When and why did you start playing with NOJO ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : I started playing with NOJO in 2002 when the organization was formed . It was important to me to be a member of NOJO because of what it represents . NOJO is a non-profit organization that preserves , educates and exposes the world to New Orleans music and culture by way of an 18-piece jazz orchestra . When I was a kid growing up in the city , it was rare to see a big band perform , and we definitely did not have an institute dedicated to preserving big band culture . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Q : What kind of satisfaction do you take in playing with a big band , compared to playing in a small group ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : Performing in a big band is much different than playing in a small group . Roles are more defined . Navigating through a piece of music with 18 musicians requires a different level of concentration and skill . As a drummer in a big band , you must be fundamentally sound to properly lead and direct the band musically . If you have bad time , are unable to set up rhythmic figures , or not able influence the music dynamically , you will be exposed . In a smaller configuration , a lot of times drummers can mask their shortcomings by overplaying. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Q : Now that you 're NOJO 's artistic director , what has that meant for you and the band ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : This position has taught me how to be a good administrator , leader and musician . I now have to work with a staff and board , create budgets , curate concert seasons , develop educational programming , create budgets , develop recording concepts , work with booking agents and managers , rehearse and tour the band and whatever is required for us to be successful as an organization . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For the band , it has obviously meant a change in leadership style , musical content and an overall different approach . I&amp;rsquo ; ve always been a team player and I look to the musicians in the orchestra for guidance and I value their input musically . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Q : What makes NOJO stand out , compared to other well-known U.S. big bands ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : I guess we can ask what makes New Orleans different than any other city in the U.S. ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; NOJO is comprised of 18 musicians that live and work in New Orleans , and contribute to the local music scene and the advancement of our culture in the States and around the world . We focus on preserving the music of New Orleans artists and we embody what New Orleans is every time we hit the stage . What other jazz orchestra does that ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Q : What music will you play in Ottawa , and why ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : I&amp;rsquo ; m really looking forward to our show in Ottawa . We will be performing the music from our new CD Songs : The Music of Allen Toussaint . Allen Toussaint fans will hear some of his biggest hits , Working in the Coal Mine , Southern Nights , Ruler of My Heart , It&amp;rsquo ; s Raining and others . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Q : I 'm interested in the New Orleans perspective on jazz as it 's played outside of where it was born . What do you think of the strands of contemporary jazz that comes out of New York , or Brooklyn , or for that matter , Europe ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : I think the music has changed over the years and I think evolution is inevitable . I believe that learning the fundamentals and history of the music is imperative to understanding how to play it . But that shouldn&amp;rsquo ; t impede advancement . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; We have many leaders that make great contributions to jazz globally through performances , leading cultural institutions and presenting jazz artists around the world . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This responsibility falls on all that are committed to providing opportunities for audiences to hear and appreciate the music and the artists that create it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; New Orleans Jazz Orchestra &lt;br&gt; When : Tuesday , Feb. 25 , 8 p.m. &lt;br&gt; Where : Shenkman Arts Centre , 245 Centrum Blvd , Orl&amp;eacute ; ans &lt;br&gt; Tickets : $58 , ( premium $65 , student $20 ) at shenkmanarts.ca &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; phum@postmedia.com &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN ARTS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span style= " font-family:Calibri ; " &gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;2677;TOOLONG ... and hope to fill NAC when Nova Scotia 's Jenn Grant **31;2712;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;2745;TOOLONG ... style= " font-family:Calibri ; " &gt;NAC preview : Play explores what happens when four people with opposing political views sit down for **29;2780;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;2811;TOOLONG ... style= " font-size:12pt ; font-family:Calibri ; " &g; ... ArtsPianist Rafael Zaldivar spins musical innovations from of his Afro-Cuban rootshttp : **35;2924;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;2961;TOOLONG ... title= " Montreal pianist Rafael Zaldivar " alt= " Montreal pianist Rafael Zaldivar " data-portal-copyright= " Mathieu Rivard " **28;2997;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1560016 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; When Rafael Zaldivar was five years old and growing up in Cuba , he took his first music lessons from his grandparents . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Now based in Montreal , Zaldivar then was decades away from becoming a Juno-nominated pianist who has worked and rubbed shoulders with some of contemporary jazz&amp;rsquo ; s biggest names . But the roots of the music that he makes today , and will perform Saturday at the National Arts Centre&amp;rsquo ; s Fourth Stage , are nonetheless connected to his earliest experiences in music . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Music offered me a unique opportunity to progressively increase my cultural introspection , &amp;rdquo ; says Zaldivar , who is in his mid-30s. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At the Fourth Stage , Zaldivar will present his Afro-Cuban Revival band , a sinewy , earthy project that melds the rhythms of his homeland and Africa with the sophistication of jazz . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 640 " height= " 360 " src= " https : **34;3027;TOOLONG ... frameborder= " 0 " allow= " accelerometer ; autoplay ; encrypted-media ; gyroscope ; picture-in-picture " **34;3063;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; Before Zaldivar took up the piano , he got a grounding in rhythm through percussion instruments . But eventually the piano won out . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Zaldivar says that the piano , too , is a percussion instrument , but it also offers him &amp;ldquo ; the full range of orchestration&amp;rdquo ; of rich harmony and melodies. &amp;ldquo ; It strongly appealed to me and I never gave the piano up since then . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At 13 , Zaldivar fell under the sway of some truly masterful Cuban pianists : Chucho Vald&amp;eacute ; s , Gonzalo Rubalcaba , and Gabriel Hernandez. &amp;ldquo ; They had all developed a strong voice through an Afro-Cuban rhythmic ideal in jazz composition and improvisation , &amp;rdquo ; Zaldivar says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Then , when U.S. jazz great Herbie Hancock visited Havana in 1998 , Zaldivar got a chance to speak to him . Hancock , Zaldivar says , spoke of the importance of jazz&amp;rsquo ; s bebop-based piano lineage. &amp;ldquo ; Since then , I have been involved with black-work-songs , blues , gospel , swing , and bebop songs . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Almost 20 years later , Zaldivar dug deeper into bebop through the veteran New York-based pianist and teacher . &amp;ldquo ; He completely illuminated my mind , &amp;rdquo ; Zaldivar says . &amp;ldquo ; He was a rich bible of knowledge in developing jazz roots through bebop. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; These models inspired me to understand the meaning of jazz and taught me how to try to stretch innovation out from roots , &amp;rdquo ; Zaldivar says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; By then , Zaldivar had come to Canada . He immigrated to Sherbrooke , Que. in 2005 , at the age of 22 . He completed a B.A. from the Universit&amp;eacute ; de Montr&amp;eacute ; al in 2009 , and an M.A. from McGill University in 2011. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That year , Zaldivar&amp;rsquo ; s debut disc Life Directions won two prestigious Quebec music awards &amp;mdash ; the Prix Opus and the Grand Prix Musical Archambault . In 2013 , his sophomore album , Drawing , was nominated for a Juno Award , vying for the best contemporary jazz album . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; His musical profundity and virtuosity has also afforded him opportunities to play with some cutting-edge American jazz artists , including saxophonists Steve Coleman and Greg Osby , guitarist Nir Felder , and drummers Ari Hoenig and Dan Weiss. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Zaldivar speaks philosophically about the place of music in his life . &amp;ldquo ; Music reflects the health of my soul and brings the colours of my emotional scale out of my life experiences , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In Canada , music reinforced my human values and helped me to find my place , &amp;rdquo ; he continues . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Now , I have accomplished most of my professional dreams . Music is the highlighted line that drives my healthy and successful life . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For Zaldivar , his Afro-Cuban Revival project signifies &amp;ldquo ; being conscious of what cultural background and genetic line mean to our lives . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The musical and cultural virtues that I want to share with listeners are the circularity of rhythm and the spirituality of human values through Afro-Cuban songs or prayer , &amp;rdquo ; &amp;nbsp ; he says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Rafael Zaldivar -- Afro-Cuban Revival&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;br&gt; &lt;strong&gt;When : &lt;/strong&gt; Saturday , Feb. 15 , 8:30 p.m. &lt;br&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Where : &lt;/strong&gt; NAC Fourth Stage &lt;br&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Tickets : &lt;/strong&gt; nac-cna.ca or the NAC box office &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **25;3099;TOOLONG " **32;3126;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN ARTS AND LIFE&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " http : **34;3160;TOOLONG ... preview : Fronteras lights expose the darkness of borders , barriers , surveillance culture&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;3196;TOOLONG ... crap ' : Ottawa woman who went viral for pizza box video makes cameo in Oscar-winning movie Parasite&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;3231;TOOLONG ... is getting a new food and wine festival at the Shaw Centre&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Peter HumThu , 13 Feb 2020 23:24:15 **45;3266;TOOLONG ... ArtsOttawa winter jazz preview : Saxophonist Allison Au found musical inspiration in her biracial ancestryhttp : **32;3313;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;3347;TOOLONG ... title= " Juno Award-winning saxophonist Allison Au " alt= " Juno Award-winning saxophonist Allison Au " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;3383;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 309835 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;3413;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; Allison Au says she cried a lot while writing her most ambitious work to date , which she calls Migrations Suite . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Juno-winning Toronto-based saxophonist drew upon the inspirations of her ancestry , poring over her grandparents&amp;rsquo ; photos before setting notes to paper . On her father&amp;rsquo ; s side , Au , who is 33 , is Chinese , while on her mother&amp;rsquo ; s side , she is Jewish . The result is a work that teems with lyrics telling of migration , set to the accompaniment of an expanded ensemble that combines jazz and classical elements . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Au will be playing with her quartet Saturday night at the TD Ottawa Winter Jazz Festival . While Au&amp;rsquo ; s core band doesn&amp;rsquo ; t yet have arrangements of this new work in its repertoire , the group can be expected to deliver stirring and original contemporary jazz nonetheless . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Below , Au discusses her most personal music efforts yet . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Q : When did you come up with the idea to write your Migrations Suite ? What was your goal with this work ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : When I was commissioned by the Royal Conservatory of Music and the 21C Music Festival , I was informed that my band would be premiering the music in an opening slot for Danilo P&amp;eacute ; rez&amp;rsquo ; s Global Messengers Ensemble . I intentionally tried to find a way to complement Danilo&amp;rsquo ; s Global Messengers , an ensemble that draws from various musical traditions and showcases a unique instrumentation . So I set out to find a musical theme that would be global in scope . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As I was brainstorming , I knew I wanted to address subject matter that was unique to me , something that I could share that would feel authentic and genuine . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; I didn&amp;rsquo ; t anticipate the music would become so personal . But it wasn&amp;rsquo ; t long before I realized that I could speak to my own family history , because my ancestry is international in breadth and dimension . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; By simply tracking the movements of my parents and grandparents over the last century , I could address the larger issues of displacement , relocation , lament for the loss of home , the feeling of &amp;ldquo ; foreign-ness , &amp;rdquo ; and legacy . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; By exploring my family history through music , my goal is to show how these stories are not unique . The human act of migrating is complex , but universal . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Q : How does the suite fit into your body of work ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : This suite marks a new phase in my growth as a composer . I sought to create canvasses of new textures with an expanded instrumentation that included vibraphone , violin , cello and vocals , in addition to the quartet . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Because of the limited time frame I was allocated for the performance , I forced myself to keep the pieces relatively short . So the songs , as a result , have a more through-composed feel , even though there are improvised sections within them . This is an element that varies from my other work . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Throughout the writing process , I also imagined I was writing for a classical chamber ensemble , and that really pushed me further in a new compositional direction . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Throughout , the voices of my bandmates , Todd Pentney , Jon Maharaj and Fabio Ragnelli , remained incredibly strong in my mind while composing . I could hear each of them playing the parts as I was writing them , and this aspect of my writing process has always been consistent in the creation of all my music . I really try to envision the musicians performing the work as I write it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Q : Tell me more about your compositional process . How did it draw on your family 's story ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : The writing process for this music was a very emotional one for me . I scoured my parents&amp;rsquo ; photo cabinet at home and reflected on almost every faded photograph I could find . I wanted to know who everyone was in each photo . I spent two weeks bombarding my parents and sister with questions about my grandparents , clarifying and verifying the stories I had heard as a child . Were they how I remembered them ? What changed , if anything ? The stories ? Or hearing the stories through adult ears ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Reflecting and meditating on the trauma experienced by my grandparents was painful . I cried a lot while writing this music . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Also , Migrations Suite is my first original work that prominently features a vocalist . And what&amp;rsquo ; s more , I&amp;rsquo ; m not a lyricist . So for this project , I decided to borrow the words of poets and set their words to my music . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; I made a trip to the Toronto Reference Library and spent one afternoon poring over the poetry of Indigenous Canadian , African American and other immigrant North American poets &amp;mdash ; writers who are all too familiar with the experience of &amp;ldquo ; other-ness , &amp;rdquo ; of &amp;ldquo ; foreign-ness. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; I made an effort not to use writers who speak to the exact experience of my Chinese or Jewish ancestry to show that other ethnic and religious communities have shared in the same experience as my family . I intentionally wanted to show the universality of the experience of these complex issues . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Q : Have your parents heard this music ? If so , what do they think ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : Yes ! My parents were able to attend the premiere last Saturday at Koerner Hall . It was so special to me to have them there . They told me they both loved it . I&amp;rsquo ; m not exactly sure if they hear their lives in the music per se , but they told me they really enjoyed the music as a sonic journey . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Overall , I think they were thrilled I would be inspired to write something inspired by our family story . They were really happy that I wanted to honour my ancestry in this way . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Q : How do you think this work resonates for others who have different family stories ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : If not us or our own family , we all know someone who is from somewhere else . Especially in Canada . Living in a country that prides itself on opening its doors to newcomers , the stories of migration are so prevalent . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; I think the work resonates with anyone who has either endured the immigrant experience firsthand or deeply understands what it means to leave your home , leave behind family , learn a new language , feel alienated and alone , endure prejudice and discrimination and forge a new home in a new land or community . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It is joy and pain , fear and excitement , regret and optimism . This is the human experience . This is universal . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Allison Au Quartet &lt;br&gt; TD Ottawa Winter Jazz Festival &lt;br&gt; When : Saturday , Feb. 1 , 10:30 p.m. &lt;br&gt; Where : Arts Court Theatre &lt;br&gt; Tickets : ottawajazzfestival.com &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; phum@postmedia.com &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **33;3449;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;3484;TOOLONG ... things you need to know about the 2020 TD Ottawa Winter Jazz Festival&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;3519;TOOLONG ... Peter Hum sifts through the three-night event 's 17 concerts for highlights . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; 1 ) Joel Frahm will be playing &amp;mdash ; not once , but twice . Simply put , the Brooklyn-based saxophonist is a world-class musician who always deploys his virtuosic technique in the service of unfettered , hyper-melodic improvising . But you knew that already if you heard his majestic playing last summer on the TD Ottawa Jazz Festival&amp;rsquo ; s main stage in pianist Brad Mehldau&amp;rsquo ; s quintet , or later that night at the festival&amp;rsquo ; s jam session . U.S. singer-songwriter Becca Stevens smartly and movingly fuses folk , pop and jazz better than anyone else , and would be a star if the music world were more fair and less ruled by lowest common denominators . Stevens plays with her band at the Ottawa Art Gallery at 9 p.m .
